speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Winters (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: WHEAT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SALE UNDER AGREEMENT WITH CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to inform hon. members that the Canadian Wheat Board, following prolonged negotiations in Canton, has succeeded in concluding a sales contract with mainland China to provide for the export of two million long tons, 5 per cent more or less, of wheat to be shipped from January through October, 1968.
This contract is under the provisions of the third long term agreement with China and consists of No. 1, 2 and 3 northern wheat and a small quantity of Durum wheat.
Assuming that the full tolerance is taken, the sale amounts to 78.4 million bushels. Including the contract covered by this announcement, total sales under the third long term agreement amount to 4.7 million tons or approximately 177 million bushels.
The long term agreement provides for a minimum of 4J and a maximum of 7J million tons over the three year period commencing August 1, 1966, with the amounts for each year to be negotiated separately. As in the previous contracts, payment terms for sales under the long term agreement are 25 per cent cash when each vessel is loaded, and the balance of 75 per cent in 18 months, with interest. The deferred payment provision is made possible by a guarantee to the Canadian Wheat Board by the government of Canada.
I know all hon. members will join with me in extending to the wheat board our warmest congratulations on their good work in reaching agreement on a matter which is of such importance to the Canadian economy.

Mr. Speaker, I think I can speak on behalf of all members of the house when I say that we welcome the long term agreement made with the People's Republic of China. The interesting point about this agreement is that China is taking more than the minimum amounts of 27053-3351
wheat and thus maintaining its intention which was declared as far back as 1961.
However, I think I should point out two things to the minister. One is that the Chinese are very astute and able bargainers, and undoubtedly the length of time taken over these negotiations indicates that they are determined that any faux pas made by this government and by other governments in connection with the wheat price would work to the advantage of the Chinese. Through lack of foresight on this government's part we agreed to a GATT arrangement with respect to grains that will not take effect until July 1, 1968. We were no longer protected by the international wheat agreement which, so far as price guarantees were concerned, died on August 1, 1967. The wheat farmers of the world were without the protection of a floor or ceiling price. The price of wheat, owing to the actions of merchants on the Chicago and Kansas City exchanges, dropped to around 23 cents and 24 cents per bushel.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
As is their right, the Chinese have taken full advantage of this drop in price. At the same time it must be pointed out loudly and clearly that the western wheat farmers will place the blame for this drop in price squarely on the shoulders of the government.
My second point, to which I referred partially yesterday, is that no nation has been more considerate to Canada in these long term agreements than China has been. In 1961 we asked the Chinese if they would not consider setting up a trade office in Canada to facilitate the exchange of business relationships between our private business sector and their crown corporations or government selling agencies. The Chinese agreed to do that, and I did not find out until 1964 why the pledge which our government had given to the Chinese was not fulfilled. I conveyed my intelligence about this matter to the then minister of trade and commerce but to this day a pledge that was given by one government in Canada has not been carried out by a subsequent government. That is why so long as this government persists in failing to carry out something that is very necessary to keep intact the good will between our two nations, I intend to continue to bring this

December 12, 1967
Wheat sale to China
point up. It is only a small matter, but if we do as we promised we shall show the Chinese people that we accept them in the world of nations where we trade with them regardless of their politics, their religion or their colour. I think it is very important to make this kind of gesture, and I hope the Minister of Trade and Commerce will move on this matter as quickly as possible and that he will not procrastinate any longer.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the announcement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce will be welcome in western Canada, and since his announcement has implications for the entire Canadian economy it will be welcome across the country. It is particularly welcome at a time of growing despondency in western Canada. Our farmers were worried that wheat exports would not be increased. Over many months grain has been building up at terminal positions. Since that grain, which was ready for export, has not been moved, the effect of the build up has been felt all the way back to the country elevators. As a result the wheat producers of western Canada have become increasingly dissatisfied and disillusioned.
Some aspects of the transaction which the minister has announced to the house are not clear to me. I am not clear about the details as to price and as to the grades of wheat that are in the main to be accepted by the Chinese pursuant to the latest agreement. I thought, as did many people, that, under the terms of the master agreement we might face considerable difficulty in exporting wheat to the Chinese, since in this year's crop we had an oversupply of high grades of wheat and an undersupply, considering the demands of the market, of low grades of wheat. I take for granted that these problems have been resolved in the transaction which the minister has referred to.
In conclusion I wish to endorse the closing remarks of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, in which he pointed out, as he has done on several previous occasions, that the continuation of Canadian wheat sales to China, which are crucial, have a lot to do with government policy concerning whether or not China should be allowed to establish a trading office in this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF OIL EXPLORATION PROGRAM IN ARCTIC ISLANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce a new, major step in northern development. About 18 months ago we announced to hon. members the northern grants program to develop mineral resources. This program assisted Canadian companies operating in the territories by way of grants toward exploration costs.
December 12, 19G7

Indications of oil deposits in the Arctic have been known for many years. Geologists have long recognized the potential of the area. The presence of thousands of feet of sediments combined with occurrences of oil sands and other indications of hydrocarbons have produced optimistic assessments. The prospect of major pools of oil in this region will now be tested by a Canadian company.
Using the provision of the northern grants program a new Canadian company, Panarctic Oils Limited, will invest not less than $20 million on a three year oil exploration program in the Arctic islands. Panarctic is a consortium which includes leading Canadian oil and mining companies.
The government of Canada has joined the consortium. Industry and government have co-operated in a unique relationship to undertake the exploration necessary to develop the potential of a special and unusual region.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
The participating companies will invest $11 million and the government $9 million over a three year period. In return for this participation of 45 per cent of the exploration costs the people of Canada, through the government, will hold 45 per cent of the common shares and 45 per cent of the preference shares the company will issue. The government's share has been budgeted for within the existing five year program for northern development.
Should the program be extended and the exploration investment be raised to $30 million or more, the government retains the option of extending its interest pro rata. In addition, special provisions in the agreements empower the government to control the transfer of shares and therefore the degree of Canadian ownership and control.
I have a list of the 20 participants and if I may, Mr. Speaker, I would ask leave that they be inserted in the records.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF OIL EXPLORATION PROGRAM IN ARCTIC ISLANDS
speechtext:
The companies will acquire stock in Panarctic concurrently with the government. On the basis of stock ownership as of December 1 the company was 56 per cent owned by Canadians; with government participation it is now 76 per cent.
The company will have interests in approximately 44 million acres of oil land through a series of agreements with the original permit holders. As a result some 60 small companies, the majority of which are Canadian, will see their interests explored under Canadian auspices. Without Panarctic many of these interests might have been lost to their Canadian owners because of their inability to finance exploration. Panarctic will control just over 63 per cent of the Arctic lands regarded as potential oil and gas bearing acreage.
Panarctic's interest in this vast acreage varies under the agreement between 50 per cent and 90 per cent. If the full $30 million program should be completed the non-resident interest in these Canadian oil lands will be less than 20 per cent.
It is gratifying, Mr. Speaker, to tell the house that this great Canadian resource potential will be assessed by Canadians and that the majority ownership will rest with Canadians. This is a unique project. It brings together a large number of interests in the private sector on the one hand and the government on the other, under one organization capable of effecting the economies so necessary in the north. Here we have a new development approach in this special region of the country, with optimistic prospects for building the economy of our northern lands.

December 12, 1967
Northern Affairs
This is a risk venture. There is no certainty oil will be found. It is certain no oil will be found unless exploration is carried out. This announcement signals the beginning of search, not certain success. I am sure the house will agree with me that the possibilities are so attractive that this venture is wholly justified.
The discovery of oil would be of immense benefits. It could conceivably change Canada's role ultimately from that of a net importer of oil to that of a net exporter, with all the consequent benefits to our balance of payments position and our economic well being generally. In that happy event new oil reserves would represent a welcome addition to the reserves of the western world in the light of the increasing demand for oil.
Marketing of any new oil found in Canada would of course take place within the framework of co-operation which has characterized our relationships with our major trading partners in this and other areas. If this venture is successful, all of Canada will be enriched.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the last three or four years those of us who sit on this side of the house have not had too many opportunities to say good words about what the government has done, but this is one such occasion. To make my point very loud and clear I would like to remind all hon. members of the house that the fundamental function of the federal government is to provide the Canadian economic base on which our federal, provincial and municipal governments can afford the services that our people want.
The announcement we have heard from the minister today is a classic example of the type of thing that should be done by this government, and should have been done by it over the last four years. To put the matter into perspective-and I hope all Canadians hear this-it is now estimated, as the result of several studies, that the energy demands of the world will increase over four times by the end of the century, in other words in less than 33 years. To meet that fourfold increase in demand it is estimated that the share of oil and gas will climb from 50 per cent of the current consumption to 55 per cent of the increased consumption.
This means we have to make tremendous efforts in all oil bearing regions of the world to prove the reserves available to meet this
[Mr. Laing.l
fantastically growing demand. At the present time, for example, it is estimated that to maintain a proper balance to meet currently known demands our reserves should be a certain proportion of our known demands. Using very round figures, we have to go out in the world at the present time and multiply our oil reserves by five times to provide that correct balance between reserves and demand. In the case of natural gas we will have to go out and prove up reserves 15 times over the presently known reserves to meet the demand by the end of the century.
This statement by the minister is the first indication I have seen of an effort on the part of this government to play its part in proving these reserves. The previous government did much in that regard by accepting the fact that to meet this great demand for energy it had to have some form of inventory of our resources. Without listing the programs on which we embarked I could give just a few examples to indicate the coherent approach we took after we had won the control of the resources at the bottom of the sea under international law in 1958.
These examples include a polar continental shelf exploration program which is still going on, the extension of hydrographic surveys, the setting up of an oceanography institute, and the oil and gas regulations which were put through in 1959 which dealt with the handling of these reserves in our northern areas and at the bottom of the sea off our coasts. This type of coherent program is the forerunner of the type of program the minister has just announced, because the philosophy is the same.
I should like to point out for the minister's personal benefit something I am sure he knows. In making an announcement such as he has made he is acting in conformity with a wealth of precedent in Canada. I do not want to go back as far as the C.P.R. but starting in the year 1911 there was a man on our treasury benches who had brought into this house a roads to resources program which passed this house but was turned down by the Senate. It was the same minister from Alberta, Mr. Lougheed, who brought in the program for exploration of the Arctic islands. The minister today is acting in conformity with this historic precedent.
I should like to say just a word or two about the agreement itself. With our geography and the economics being what they are, I do not think we have any choice but to accept the fact that in the northern area, particularly the Arctic islands and the land
December 12, 1967

off the shores at the bottom of the sea, the government must take the lead. In this particular proposal we have the device of the government of Canada sharing in the equity because of the risk being taken. This precedent is now being followed by nearly all the provinces. Now that the federal government has gone into this device, it corrects what I think was wrong with the exploration program or the northern grants program announced some time ago in the house. Now with the taxpayer's money going into one of these projects he has some chance of seeing his money coming back. He knows that in this type of proposal he will see it coming back manyfold.
The second point I should like to make about the agreement deals with the question of public participation. The minister in his statement pointed out that the government would have control over the transfer of shares. I wish to remind the minister that we have in effect at the present time in the oil and gas regulations dealing with the Yukon Territory, the Northwest Territories and the continental shelf a regulation which says that if any company moves to ownership in the production of wealth in this area, that company must be formed as a Canadian company and must put its shares as a public company on the stock exchanges of this country. This is the way the Canadian people will be able to participate in the ownership of these resources. Under that regulation the government and any other private company will be allowed to buy the shares if they offer enough money on the open market. This regulation is absolutely fundamental to the ownership of wealth by Canadians in a positive as opposed to a negative way.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
Having made these two points I hope private enterprise, which is running this company, will operate it on sound business procedures. I am sure they will. I have in my possession a list of the companies, and I know their reputation for being hard fisted. I am sure they will watch every economic point in the development procedure. I hope these people will read my statement and get clear in their minds the fact that good practice requires the use of the tender system when they are looking for transportation to do these things in the north, so that ultimately the common carriers in Canada will be given a chance to participate in this work.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a point I am not too happy to make but feel
Northern Affairs
that I should. Some time ago one of our members, the hon. member for Yukon, asked this question in the house:
Has the government engaged in discussions with private oil exploration and/or drilling companies with a view to participating in the establishment of a crown corporation for the purpose of channelling public and private investment funds into exploration of the Arctic archipelago?
This question was answered on November 13. The question and the answer appear at page 4174 of Hansard for that date. The answer was "No". Here we have an example of government deviousness that we are trying to do away with in this house if we are to restore confidence in government.

Mr. Speaker, I hope my remarks will fall within your proscription and not be unduly lengthy. At the outset I should like to say that as interesting as the statement was it is not particularly newsworthy or new, in that almost all the comments the minister has made appeared in a newspaper yesterday in an article by Jock Osier of the Financial Times news service emanating from Toronto. I do not care whether information of this sort comes to us by way of statements on motions or by way of press releases outside the house, but something of this sort which could have a bearing on the position of those who want to speculate on the market should be kept confidential until such time as the government discloses it in a proper way. I am not sure whether this will have any influence, but prior information of this sort could work to the disadvantage of the desires of the government.
It has long been our contention that the government has a particular role to play in the development and exploitation of the resources of this nation. The minister called this project unique, but I think it might more appropriately be described as one which recognizes the sound thinking and policies emanating from this party to which I belong over the years. I hope the government will not look upon this as unique in the sense that it will be the only one of its kind in the history of Canada, because there is ample

December 12, 1967
Northern Affairs
opportunity in other fields of activity for government participation of a similar nature.
Industry when left to itself operates primarily on the basis of the need for profit and its responsibility to shareholders. Any benefit which accrues to the nation and its people or the employees from the operations of such a company is secondary to this first need. It is the government's role to protect the rights of the people in respect of their position in the economy. The 45 per cent ownership figure mentioned by the minister suggests that action can be taken to control the movement of shares so this company can operate in a way to protect and enhance the position of Canadians.
There is one factor in respect of the number of directors of the board, not mentioned by the minister, which is of some concern. Perhaps at a later date he will let us know what this means in terms of who shall be members of the board. As the minister knows, in the development of the north we must concern ourselves not only with jobs for individuals but with social aspects and the total economy. I am sure the minister is aware of this, in view of statements he has made on numerous occasions.
In this regard we cannot relate the development of the north only to industries involved in extraction of resources, or industries which exist for the purpose of taking raw materials for export out of the area or out of the nation, which is even worse. We must concentrate on secondary manufacturing and processing industries which will process the raw materials into finished products in order that the maximum benefit will accrue to the nation and to the area. We have passed the stage when we should continue to export raw materials at a certain price and import finished products made from those materials at five or six times that price. When we do this we in effect export jobs and hinder our position in respect of the balance of payments.

Mr. Speaker, the measure announced by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Laing) is a step forward taken by the government.
The minister announced that instead of substituting itself to private enterprise, the government is taking measures to assist it, which is a commendable aim. Besides, this is what our party has always maintained, that is, a government exists, not in order to substitute itself to private enterprise but to help the latter to develop the natural resources of a country like ours. The minister's statement makes clear that the government is about to foster the economic activity of Canada.

The participating companies will invest $11 million and the government $9 million over a three year period.

This is a risk venture and I would say that the future of this country belongs to those who are not afraid to take risks. Mr. Speaker, that policy is clearly a Canadian policy, truly progressive and

progressist, because 56 per cent of the shares of Panarctic Oils Limited will be held by Canadians, and through the participation of the government, the company will be Canadian-owned in a proportion of 76 per cent.

I shall be very brief, Mr. Speaker. First of all I wish to thank the minister for sending us a copy of the statement so we had an opportunity to look at it.
I have some reservations in connection with the proposal made by the minister. First of all, due to the situation in which Canada finds itself today in connection with the spending of money, the amount of money to be expended in this connection should be a consideration in deciding whether to go ahead with the plan outlined by the minister. Also, I think this proposal encourages what the municipalities call ribbon development.
In other words I believe we are being premature in what we are proposing to do. If we are to develop the north country I think it should be on the basis of a gradual development. If this were done I think the proven oil policies of the provinces would be sufficient to carry out the development and exploration. In that way development would occur in a very, very logical manner, rather than the situation under a policy that is superficially imposed, which I believe will be the case with this one. Therefore I believe we would be wise to take a close look at what we are doing in the way of precedent in connection with the whole question of development of the north country.

be strong enough to carry out the new mandate, and there is another opinion that perhaps the force should be enlarged. No agreement has yet been reached because the matter has not come before the security council.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, December 11, consideration of the motion of Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 11, 1967, I had the honour to participate in the debate which had been resumed on the budget presented on the 1st of June and to make my own comments.
I mentioned, among other things, that the spectre of inflation was more and more threatening in this country and that the fight
The Budget-Mr. F. E. Leblanc started by this government should be intensified and should get the support and cooperation of every level of government, in short, of the whole community and of every citizen.
I also mentioned that the government, on account of the urgency of the situation, could be compelled to take drastic steps if conditions did not improve. Among those measures, I mentioned the possibility of levying a special and temporary tax.
At this stage, Mr. Speaker, I will pause to say that strangely enough, that speech was not mentioned a single time in the information media-except, as far as I know, in the November 1967 issue of La Revue du transport routier du Quebec

while the bills on money and postage stamps were loudly publicized throughout the country, due to the opposition members.
At this time, I think it would be advisable and wise to stop and ask ourselves whether this country has not reached the saturation point in its fiscal and tax system.
I find my answer in an article published in the Ottawa Citizen on the 6th of December 1967. I quote:

Certainly our income tax levels are lower than those of most other western nations. But income tax levels are only a fragment of the total picture.
The yardstick we are concerned with is total taxation at all levels of government. The basis for international comparison is the percentage of gross national product-the total value of goods and services produced in the country in a year- that is absorbed by governments.
One of the most recent compilations, for the 1964 taxation year, looks like this:
Total taxes as
Country	percent of GNP
France	37.6
Sweden	36.6
West Germany	34.9
Norway	34.3
United Kingdom	29.4
Belgium	28.8
Denmark	28.1
Canada	27.3
U.S.	27.1
[Translation1
You will notice with me that Canada ranks eighth on this list.
Since we precede by 0.2 per cent our main competitor and supplier, the United States, we must surely continue to ask ourselves, and this seriously, whether our country has not reached the saturation point as far as taxes and taxation are concerned?

December 12, 1967

The Budget-Mr. F. E. Leblanc

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I ask the
hon. member a question? If he really believes that the Canadian people has reached a saturation point concerning tax increases, should he not denounce his government for these increases that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) imposed as a result of his last budget?

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the hon. member will let me finish my speech, he will see that my argument takes his question into account.
The special and temporary tax which I mentioned in my speech of October 11 last has now been proposed by the Minister of Finance and has been set at 5 per cent of the amount of the basic tax assessed on an individual in excess of $100. This surtax will take effect on January 1 and would remain until we have completed the transition to a slower rate of growth of expenditures or until economic and financial conditions call for a change in our fiscal policy.
Knowing the honesty and intellectual integrity of the Minister of Finance, I am satisfied that this tax will really be temporary, and I am sure that the minister is willing to give his word to all Canadian taxpayers that this is a temporary measure which will last only as long as the needs remain and which will be withdrawn as soon as the above-mentioned conditions are restored.
I note with pleasure that this surtax does not apply to small wage-earners until the following annual income has been reached: $2,500 for an unmarried taxpayer, $3,500 for married people without any dependent and $4,000 for a married taxpayer with two children entitled to family allowances.
If you look at the tables showing how the 5 per cent surtax applies, you will realize also that the taxpayer whose annual income does not exceed $10,000 will not have to pay a huge amount in additional tax.
In fact, an unmarried taxpayer will pay about 17 cents a week, a married man without children, 14 cents and a married taxpayer with two children entitled to family allowances, about 12 cents. Therefore, the main burden of the surtax will be borne by the taxpayers whose income exceeds $10,000. The maximum amount payable by that category of taxpayers will be $600.
In my speech of October 11 last, I said this:
At the present time, those who earn less than $5,000 pay too much tax compared to the other taxpayers, and the Minister of Finance should make the required adjustment.
[Mr. Leblanc (Laurier) .1
Still, the full burden should not be placed on the shoulders of those citizens who earn from $5,000 to $10,000, thereby creating another injustice while wanting to remedy the first error.
I am gratified to find that in this 5 per cent surtax at least, the principle laid down in my speech has been observed and I hope that in the tax reform being considered by the Minister of Finance, the experts who advised him will continue along the same lines so as to maintain this principle of equity for all taxpayers, a principle based on a scale which is better balanced with the revenue.
It goes without saying that a tax increase is never popular. The Minister of Finance surely did not take his personal interest into consideration when he presented his budget on November 30. He and his colleague, the Minister of National Revenue and President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Benson) are showing an exemplary courage and a rare strength of character in the present circumstances by asking the people to tighten their belt still more and to enter a period of austerity.
The past has shown that tax increases and austerity programs are not wise measures from the political point of view in Canada, because they are always very unpopular.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
However, the intellectual development of our population which is the result of better schooling and an improved system of education in my opinion makes it possible for Canadians to understand better today that these measures were necessary to check the disastrous consequences of inflation. All of us in this house must stop being demagogues and explain to the people that these measures will stop the inflationary rise in prices and in the cost of living, which endanger our economic stability. At the same time, we must stop making too many demands on the capital market and, instead, pay for our social security programs.
According to a recent Gallup poll, the federal government is bluntly blamed for the present high cost of living. More than 6 adult Canadians out of 10, that is 65 per cent, believe that Ottawa could have done more to stop the price spiral. It is in Quebec that you find the largest number of dissatisfied citizens in this regard, that is 70 per cent. In western Canada, it is 68 per cent, while in Ontario, this percentage decreases to 60 per cent. Here is the question which was asked:
Do you think that the government could have done more to stop the rising cost of living? Or do you think that this rise is due to other factors over which the government has no control?
December 12, 1967

This poll must open our eyes and lead us to wonder whether the federal government is actually the only one responsible for inflation, in brief whether it is the only one to spend large sums of money in Canada.
It is a fact that our expenditures have increased by 92 per cent between 1957 and 1967, but this is about the same percentage of our gross national product as 10 years ago, and a little below that of 5 years ago. During that period, we have lowered our taxation rate in favour of the provinces, while the expenditures of provincial and municipal governments have increased at a faster rate than federal expenditures. In fact, they have increased from 11.1 to 18.6 per cent of our gross national product, while federal expenditures have remained at a fairly constant level during this period, that is 16.4 in 195667 and 16.8 in 1967.
Of course, there is no question of blaming the provinces and the municipalities for this, because they have been facing increasing responsibilities with the years. It is just a matter of setting out the facts in order to enlighten the people as to those actually responsible for inflation.
We should not forget, either, the important and ever-growing role of the trade unions with respect to wages increases, and consequently, production costs and price increases. Surely there is a need for greater restraints in regard to increases in prices, wages and other sources of cash income, such as rents, dividends and interests.
Another factor which has also contributed to inflation is related to the large corporations. During the last years, we have seen that profits of Canadian corporations were definitely too high. Today, we realize that this situation is improving, but I think this inflationary factor should be neither denied nor ignored.
In addition, we have seen land and real estate speculators often realizing exorbitant profits, and I am sure that such feverish speculation has definitely helped to bring about the inflation problem we are experiencing today.
Finally, we should add perhaps that Canada is quite sensitive to the reactions of the world markets and especially to the reactions of the American market. It has been shown, beyond the shadow of a doubt, that the inflationary period is not a phenomenon particular to Canada but that, on the contrary, several countries, at the present time, feel that calamity more severely than we do and,
The Budget-Mr. F. E. Leblanc for instance, I simply have to mention England.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I come to the conclusion that the rise in the cost of living is due, for a major part, to factors over which the government has no control.
The Minister of Finance has devoted a special paragraph to his program of fiscal reform as a result of the Carter report. He tells us that, due to the representations of the Canadian people with regard to that report, the government considers that our taxation system should undergo considerable reform which should take into account the needs of the country but should not interfere with the progress and proper development of the Canadian economy. Our present system is not completely and absolutely bad and it is impossible to reject it all, although it has often been patched up haphazardly over the years at the whim of successive ministers of finance. It is high time it was completely reviewed and the required solutions were applied, in keeping, to a certain extent, with the recommendations of the Carter commission.
I wish to take this opportunity to protest a third time in the house against the capital gains tax, for all the reasons given in my two earlier speeches, but I will refrain from stating them again, so as not to extend this debate unduly.
When the white paper on tax reform is drafted, I hope the minister will take into consideration all the protests made against the capital gains tax and that, in addition, he will consider the possibilities I have already mentioned in the house, in order to encourage Canadian investors to contribute more to the development of our natural resources, that is to increase from 20 to 50 per cent the exemption on dividends paid by Canadian companies; to raise tax exemptions on research costs, to raise tax exemptions for companies developing natural resources and particularly in the case of Canadian companies; to allow companies to deduct from taxable income double the costs incurred by them for the education of their active or unemployed workers; to allow the head of a family to deduct from his income the money spent on the education of his children; to take the necessary measures so that the Minister of National Revenue will completely abandon the field of succession duties or tax on donations so as to enable the provinces to legislate exclusively in these areas; to take a more realistic attitude and raise the statutory

December 12, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Starr exemption on charitable gifts and medical expenses from $100 to $200.
Naturally, I leave it up to the fertile imagination of the minister and his experts to find the other formulas required to stimulate the Canadian economy suffering at the present time from a temporary trouble which might prove disastrous if it becomes chronic.
I am convinced that the Liberal government will find early remedies and that all Canadians, whatever their racial origin, will be able to face with equanimity a higher standard of living in a geographic, political and economic unity with social and cultural diversity.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate on the budget or, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) has dubbed it, the financial message, I want to congratulate him on his performance in setting new records. I must say that they are very outstanding records indeed. I doubt that in the near future or for a long time to come any minister of finance will be able to match the outstanding records he has been able to achieve in such a short time. We here who are closest to the affairs of government, and Canadians generally, have come to know him as the minister who has set records.
We have come to know him as the minister who has the highest interest rates in the history of this country, who has the highest cost of living in the history of this country, who has the highest expenditures in the history of this country, who has the highest prices, who brought about the highest taxation, who brought about the highest inflation, who has had the highest budgets, who has introduced more budgets than anybody else in such a comparatively short time, and who has made a mess of housing in this country. Mr. Speaker, what has Canada done to deserve all this?

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In my opinion this budget is an example of sloppy financing. It is not even a budget because the minister himself has termed it a financial message. It is just a taxation measure tacked on to taxation measures that we already have before us. We did not even have a white paper preceding it. Under this government budgets have become casual things, brought in on a haphazard, hit-or-miss basis. All that Canadians have

learned from this exercise is that the government is fiscally unfit. What we are asking it for is a return to fiscal fitness.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
We are asking that he let us have expenditures related to need and bearing some relation to objectives. Let us know what the objectives are, let us have priorities, and let us have some order in government expenditures. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has made the point that the government has so tied its hands by uncontrolled and unco-ordinated expenditures that it now has no room for the essential needs of this country.
In these days of bilingualism I should like to refer to Lafontaine's fable about the grasshopper and the ant. This government has been the grasshopper. All summer long it has played about. The members of the government brought in a June budget full of sunshine and light; they gave no thought to the cold winds of December. But like the grasshopper in the fable they come knocking at the taxpayers' door in December begging for a handout.
New taxes are being levied for one simple reason and one simple purpose, to meet the bills which the government has run up and cannot pay because it can no longer borrow owing to the lack of confidence. This is the only reason for this financial message and the additional taxes imposed on the people of this country. The government has lost the confidence of those people from whom it has borrowed money in the past. These people have now dictated to the government that it must impose additional taxation on the people in order to restore their confidence in the government so that it can go to the market again. I would not be surprised if they dictated the terms of the taxation and the areas of taxation because only the small taxpayer is feeling the impact of the taxes contained in this financial message.
The Minister of Finance indicated that the government would be cutting back on housing by slowing down direct lending. This will produce a disastrous effect on construction and on the ability of Canadians to acquire housing. They have removed one dollar of the subsidy on hogs and lambs. It had to be done; their extravagance left them no choice. But why should Ontario and Quebec farmers pay for the wild-eyed schemes of the government? They cut $480,000 from the estimate for the Company of Young Canadians for next year. Mr. Speaker, why wait until the
December 12, 1967

economy is against the wall? Why did the minister not impress upon his colleagues the facts of life long before now, long before the cold days of December? Why did he wait until December to tell them what he should have told them in June of this year?
The Leader of the Opposition in his remarks last week shot down in flames the spurious claims of future savings by this government. For the first time in a democratic world and in a democratic form of government the people and parliament have been told what is going to happen in the next fiscal year. Of course this is not the first time the Liberal party has offered a pie in the sky, Mr. Speaker, but I believe it is the first time they have tried to cut it while it was still in the sky. The government finds itself moving in an increasingly restricted area. I am greatly disturbed by the indications. I know that the municipalities all across Canada will be disturbed that there is no program of assistance for them. The majority of our population is now living in the cities. When one looks at this budget one concludes that the government is completely unaware of this fact.
At this time I should like to refresh the minister's memory with a reference to the submission of the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities on November 6. The mayors fully supported the reference in the report of the Economic Council of Canada as follows:
-there has long been widespread concern about the mounting deficiencies of our cities and the heavy backlogs of essential improvements.
Shortages and inadequacy of urban housing, traffic and transport problems, air and water pollution, the confused jumble of conflicting land uses, decaying neighbourhoods and monotonous suburbs, urban poverty and social disturbance, steadily rising property tax burdens and the frustrations of municipal administration-
One of the most serious of those frustrations is the financial strait-jacket in which the municipalities find themselves. The problems enumerated which affect municipalities also affect 70 per cent of our population living in urban areas. Yet this government seems completely unaware of the urban problems inasmuch as there is no provision in this budget to deal with these matters. Instead of moving to produce results in the field of housing and urban renewal and deal with some of the other problems the government is slowing down its already lethargic pace in these fields.
It is my intention, Mr. Speaker, to be as constructive as possible in dealing with the
The Budget-Mr. Starr present chaotic situation in which we find ourselves because, after all, as Canadians we are embroiled in this chaotic condition brought about by the government. We must face up to it and try to do the best we can under these circumstances. Even the minister will admit that the fact that the government has to come along now and ask for money within six months of a full budget which was followed by a reassuring statement in October, just two months ago, is an indication of uncertainty on its part. I say, Mr. Speaker, that Canadians generally are fed up with paying through the nose for the extravagance of this government.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
All across the country people cannot afford to buy homes. If they could afford to buy them, there are not enough to meet the demand. If they do buy them the price of everything necessary to maintain a home is sky high. If they do not buy a home they must rent and rentals are sky high. They can go into a high-rise apartment and pay a high-rise rent. If they have anything left the minister takes it away in the form of taxes. The government is spending $11 billion this year and Canadians right across this country are asking: What are we getting for it? The government has reduced the defence forces, but now we find that the reduced forces cost more than the expanded forces.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
The minister said that he was cutting down by increasing expenditures by 4.5 per cent. This is the way he has been cutting down all along. The government has been following a policy of inconsistency. In April, 1965, they reduced taxes by 10 per cent. In March, 1966, they increased taxes, and in December, 1966, they increased the old age security and sales tax. In June, 1967, they took the tax off tranquilizers and in December, 1967, they are increasing taxes again. They have not yet put the tax back on tranquilizers. We are now living in a high cost, high tax and high spending economy because of the government's inability to deal with the situation.
The minister has lost control of inflationary tendencies in the country because he cannot control inflation in his own government's spending. The government is in trouble because of their own lack of restraint. They have once more had to increase taxes because of their inability to meet their obligations.

December 12, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Starr
The Minister of Finance is now in a position where he has been forced to increase taxes at a time when unemployment has risen and there is a softening in the economy. Lay-offs have been spreading across the country. We in the opposition have brought this to the attention of the government and have inquired as to what action they are prepared to take to soften the blow of unemployment and provide other jobs. Prosperity in this country is being siphoned off, and some who have never reached prosperity have had their situation worsened by the heavy indirect taxation caused by inflation.
The problem we must deal with is that of rising costs and prices. The governor of the Bank of Canada has warned us about this, as has the Minister of Finance. Everyone is concerned except the minister's colleagues.
Housing is an integral part of this nation's economic and social health. Nothing is more indicative of the government's inefficiency than the way in which they have created havoc in respect of housing. Again this year we are going to be 25,000 houses short of the number Canadians need. The government is making available in 1967, through direct lending and limited dividend housing, close to $500 million. According to those who know, this will provide about 35,000 homes at $15,000 each. However, we need approximately 200,000 homes per year to take care of our population needs. Inflation has hit hard at the housing market by placing the price of homes beyond the reach of most Canadians. The house builders association stated in Toronto on November 30 that the cost of an average new home in metro Toronto has jumped in the past 18 months to $30,000 from $24,000. Surely in view of this the minister must realize that not many Canadians today can afford homes in that price bracket. What are they supposed to do?
The government has made mortgage money somewhat more available through high interest rates, but I cannot emphasize too strongly that this is a device to help those who are better off. Most Canadians cannot afford to buy, rent or borrow at present prices. There is no question that up until the current year the government has been using housing as an instrument to slow down the economy. In the past few months they have begun to realize they have gone too far, but it may be too late now for action to have beneficial effects in the present winter months. These are the months we should worry about, in addition to the long range 
attitude the government should take in respect of this very important matter.
The minister knows, I am sure, that there were 30,000 fewer jobs in construction as of October this year than there were a year ago. He must also know that the number of building permits for dwellings issued up to the end of August totalled 111,360. This is an improvement over last year but it is still far from encouraging in view of the tremendous backlog of housing demand and need which the government has allowed to grow because of its inactivity in this field.
Let me also point out that industrial production is not picking up as it should. In the first nine months of this year it was only up 2.7 per cent over last year. As a measure of economic growth this is not very encouraging. When the Minister of Finance presented his financial message to the people of this country the other day he showed that this government has lost touch with reality. He made the incredible statement that his policies had brought about a recovery in housing. It is true there has been a slight increase in housing activity and in private borrowing, but surely the minister must know what has happened to prices. Does he not realize what housing costs are at this time? Is he not aware that a new home in Canada is out of the reach of 75 per cent of Canadians? Has he not read the statements of the home builders association in this regard and is he not even aware of the report submitted to his own government and tabled by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) predicting only 160,000 housing starts next year? In spite of all this the minister in his financial message gave a very clear indication that one area in which he intends to cut back, is this very sensitive and needed area of social capital represented by housing. To do this at this time is nothing short of a social injustice of the worst sort.
There is one other point I must make in relation to the minister's budget statement. He is not being above board with the Canadian people when he predicates his expenditures for next year without taking medicare and the Expo deficit into account. Surely the minister cannot leave out whatever does not appeal to him. If he does so, what sort of fiscal jockeying is this? The minister knows that medicare is now part of the law of the land. The Prime Minister has said in the house over and over again that medicare is to be brought in as provided by the legislation. The question now is whether this is or is not government policy. If it is then the
December 12, 1967

minister knows full well that his figure of $10.3 billion is nothing but a joke.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

The minister should inform us.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

The government said that the whole country was waiting for it and insisted on introducing the legislation. Yet now the Minister of Finance asks if the provinces have indicated to me whether they are prepared to join the program.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I asked the question, Mr. Speaker, simply because the hon. gentleman seems to assume that everyone should know and I therefore assumed that he must know. I do not yet know what the position of the provinces may be.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the Minister of Finance does not know he had better find out soon-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We will in due course.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -because the law says that medicare will come into effect on July 1, 1968.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: No, it does not.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

speechtext:
So the minister has only about seven months in which to find out. This points up the manner in which this government is running the affairs of the country and the relationship it has with the provinces. The government boasts about co-operative federalism, but this points up that they have failed in this area also.
The Minister of Finance has said that medicare will add $500 million; yet I am told that his colleague the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson), when appearing on television just the other day, said it would cost only about $80 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, he did not. And I did not say that, Mr. Speaker. I said we would have to raise $500 million in order to pay our share, namely, half, and the Minister of
The Budget-Mr. Starr National Revenue agreed with this. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) agreed too.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If my information is wrong I certainly do not wish to accuse the minister of making that statement, but I am told that the Minister of National Revenue said on television that it would cost only $80 million. So instead of $10.3 billion the expenditures of the Minister of Finance next year will be closer to $11 billion. And what about Expo? The minister says he is going to write that off.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. gentleman wants to understand the situation. We have already raised the money for Expo; the only question is how it will be accounted for. I really feel the hon. gentleman is trying to misrepresent the very valid reasons why I excepted these two matters.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This is the first information I have received that the money has been provided for. As an ordinary Canadian and member of parliament I have been led to believe that we had to consider the Expo deficit in next year's budget.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, but just so there is some clarification here I would point out to the hon. gentleman that the money has been raised and spent. The question is, how is it to be accounted for, how much in respect of the Quebec government and how much in respect of the federal government? Until we have settled Expo accounts we wiU not know what the amount is. Moreover, we do not have to worry about this money; the money has all been raised and spent. It is simply a matter of accounting. Therefore this does not affect my cash figures.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Evidently financial provision was not complete in all its aspects because during this debate we have had to elicit more definite and detailed information from the minister, as has just been demonstrated. It is enlightening to know that Canadians will not have to pay the deficit for Expo because, as the minister says, the money has been raised and it is just a matter of bookkeeping. I am sure that Canadians as a whole will now be pleased to pay the 5 per cent surtax in view of the fact they do not have to pay anything for Expo.
This government has to stop clowning around. It has to be honest with parliament and the people in giving information as to where we are going. It is about time the

December 12, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Starr government got down to the business of running the country. I believe that the minister and the government have shown a regrettable inability to manage the fiscal affairs of this nation. So far as the Minister of Finance and his colleagues in the government are concerned it has been a case of stop and go, chop and change.
In 1962-63 the government collected $1.7 billion in income tax. In 1966-67 the government is collecting more than double that amount from the individual taxpayer. As of Thursday, November 30, the amount was even higher. The government is collecting $350 this year in personal income tax from every person employed in Canada. In sales and luxury taxes it is collecting a further $45 this year from every employed person in Canada. It is collecting a further $60 per year from every employed person in Canada in cigarette, beer and liquor taxes. As the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith), who made such a worth-while contribution when speaking on behalf of the official opposition, asked the other night: Where does it all stop?
This government is saying to Canadians: You will drink less and smoke less. You will accept an inferior standard of housing. You will pay more for necessities or do without. You will do without luxuries and accept austerity. This is in order that the government can go on with its high spending policies. On November 28 the Winnipeg Free Press had this to say:
This request- for increased taxes.
-is a naked confession of the government's repeated budgetary blunders. There would be no need for new taxes in November if Mr. Sharp had not totally misconstrued the nation's prospects in June.

The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) was quoted in the Edmonton Journal of December 16, 1963, four years ago, as saying:
We accept deficit financing providing it does what it was intended to do-put people to work.
Now we are getting deficit financing without putting people to work. In October, for example, unemployment throughout the economy was 59,000 higher than a year earlier. In manufacturing there 66,000 fewer jobs than a year earlier. In construction there were 29,000 fewer jobs than a year

December 12, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Drury will also serve to provide a background to the important new arrangement which I propose to outline this afternoon.
As hon. members will recall, one of the first programs which the Department of Industry introduced shortly after its formation was the automotive program. This program, as all hon. members know, is designed to promote growth, efficiency and employment opportunities in a most important sector of the Canadian economy. Following this my department then focused on the need to encourage and substantially increase research development and activity in Canadian industry, with the purpose of developing a technological base from which new projects and processes for world-wide markets can be developed. As a result we introduced the program for the advancement of industrial technology and also the industrial research institute program which puts universities in a position to supply research and development services to Canadian industry.
At the same time the new Industrial Research and Development Incentives Act, passed by parliament, came into effect. As members will recollect, this act, imposed upon previous measures for this purpose, makes the incentives more widely available. These three measures, I believe, go a long way toward assisting industry upgrade and expand its technological activities.
I should also mention that the Department of Industry has assumed responsibility for the shipbuilding subsidy program. This is being reintroduced on a new basis whereby the efficiency of this industry will be progressively improved. A further most impoitant program which my department has introduced, and about which I spoke this morning at the federal-provincial conference on housing is the BEAM program. This program, whose purpose is to increase the production, manufacture and use of building materials, equipment and accessories, should contribute significantly, if it continues to enjoy the support which it already has received, to a reduction in the cost of housing. [DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Sound industrial design is an increasingly essential factor in improving productivity. In this area the Department of Industry has initiated a comprehensive program including design promotion, research and product development, design education, and design information.
Finally, the adjustment assistance program which provides loans and remissions of duty

on production machinery to automotive parts producers is an important element in assisting this industry to become more efficient in order to compete on a North American basis.
Although this is not an exhaustive list, I believe it gives hon. members an over-all view of the kind of activities in which the Department of Industry is engaged. As I stated in the standing committee of the house when the estimates of the Department of Industry were examined last June, the improvement of the productivity of a major sector of our economy is a very exciting challenge. No one can dispute the difficulties of obtaining immediate and measurable results, and yet it is a task which must succeed. My department has accepted this challenge.
At this stage I should like to make a statement on a new measure which has been formulated by my department and to which I made reference earlier.

When such situations arise at present, decisions as to what rate of duty will apply must be derived from strictly formal interpretations of the law rather than giving effect to what was the probable intention of earlier legislators.
The third advantage for machinery producers is that remission of duty can be granted in respect of production parts classed under tariff item 42700-1 which are not available in Canada. While the governor in council has authority under section 273 (L) of the Customs Act to establish temporary tariff items to permit entry of production components at a free or reduced rate, the new item will provide increased flexibility in dealing with machinery components on a case by case basis. This flexibility is expected to stimulate machinery manufacturing by encouraging specialization and assisting producers to compete more effectively.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
While the major objective of the new item is to assist the development of efficient Canadian industry, the proposal has important additional advantages. This change in the machinery tariff was of great value in enabling Canada to pay for tariff concessions offered by our major trading partners in the Kennedy round. Moreover, it constitutes a major simplification in tariff administration with correspondingly greater certainty for both producers and users of machinery.
Negotiation of the machinery proposal was difficult and protracted since removing the formal class or kind distinction required that goods under tariff items being replaced which were classified as "not made" would carry higher statutory rates. In practice the effective rates would be reduced by virtue of the operations of the new remission system.
Trading partners agreed to our proposal in the end on the understanding that an overall reduction of duty would result because remission would be granted on imports of machinery not available from production in Canada. However, they insisted that in order to treat the machinery proposal as a tariff concession by Canada there be some guarantee that it would, in fact, lead to a reduction in total duties collected on the machinery involved.
As a consequence, Canada gave an undertaking that the average annual incidence of m.f.n. duty under 42700-1 would not exceed 9
[Mr. Drury.1
per cent. This undertaking is tantamount to saying that at least 40 per cent, by value, of future m.f.n. imports under 42700-1 will consist of machinery not available from production in Canada and consequently duty will not be collected on them.
I would emphasize that this undertaking does not involve any risk for Canada. Even though domestic machinery production _ is growing, a large volume of our total machinery requirements will continue to be imported and, as at present, the largest portion of such imports will comprise machinery which is not available in Canada. During recent years, about 60 per cent of the machinery imports which will be covered under 42700-1 were ruled as being of a class or kind not made in Canada. In 1966, the figure was closer to 65 per cent and this pattern is expected to remain relatively stable. Accordingly, we anticipate no difficulty whatever in meeting our commitment on	average
incidence.
Another important advantage	of the
machinery tariff proposal is that it will eliminate the use of distinctions in the customs tariff between machinery of a "class or kind made in Canada" and "not made" in respect of a major portion of our imports and thereby remove a long-standing source of appeals and litigation with corresponding problems for Canadian industry and for customs administration as well.
The pui'pose of such "class or kind" distinctions in existing machinery tariff items, as stated at the time the most important of them were introduced, was to provide for reduced rates on production machinery not directly competitive with machinery produced in Canada. Also, various statements made by ministers at that time indicate that the words "class or kind" were to be subject to practical rather than legalistic interpretation. This was the basis of customs interpretation applied until about 1950.
By that time the difference between the rates of duty for "made" and "not made" items, which had steadily widened over the years, had become a strong incentive for importers to seek ways to bring their goods within the definition of a "class or kind not made in Canada". The annual volume of imports was also increasing rapidly. Accordingly, increased tariff litigation resulted.
In broad terms, the precedents established by litigation have resulted in a gradual movement away from applying the "class or
December 12, 1967

kind" concept on the basis of practical judgment toward narrow interpretations based on explicit legal determinations. The ever-present possibility of further litigation tended to create uncertainty for machinery producers regarding those categories of machines which they could expect would be protected by the "made in Canada" rates. Similarly, importers would not be certain in respect of the duration of an existing "not made in Canada" rate.
Because of these uncertainties, as well as the costs and delays involved in litigation, both machinery producers and users have made representations over the years that a more practical approach to the original objective of the "class or kind" provisions should be developed. In fact, some of the suggestions have been quite similar to the present machinery tariff program.
While discussing the unsatisfactory aspects of "class or kind" distinctions in respect of machinery, I should also point out that trading partners have frequently objected to them as well. The reason is that low rates of duty on "not made" goods are inherently unstable and can move to protective "made in Canada" levels by administrative action without further negotiation. Thus trading partners contend they have no assurance of continued access to the Canadian market at the low rates. Indeed, they had come to the view prior to the Kennedy round that they would not regard as concessions any tariff reductions which carried a "not made in Canada" qualification.
The procedure for dealing with applications for remissions of duty on machinery is straightforward. Importers who find that their machinery requirements are not available from production in Canada may apply to the Minister of Industry for a remission of duty, either before or after actual importation takes place. These requests will be referred to a machinery and equipment advisory board, established by the governor in council pursuant to the Department of Industry Act, composed of a chairman with a broad experience in commercial policy and the deputy ministers of finance, national revenue, trade and commerce, and industry. The purpose of this board will be to advise the Minister of Industry regarding the eligibility of machinery for remission of duty in accordance with the provisions of item 427001. The Minister of Industry will, in turn, advise the governor in council who will have final authority in granting remission.
The Budget-Mr. Drury
The machinery and equipment advisory board will proceed on a practical basis rather than the present legalistic and formal approach. Its findings will be based on facts of the case and on practical considerations. In evaluating applications, the board will be assisted by the specialized branches of the Department of Industry which will carry out the factual and analytic back-up work.
In considering applications for remission, the advisory board will have regard for two basic tests. First, it will want to know whether the machinery being imported is available from production in Canada and, second, it will wish to satisfy itself that it is in the public interest to recommend that a remission of duty be granted. The criterion of availability in Canada is to be understood as follows: Machinery is to be deemed available in Canada if at least one manufacturer has proven capability to manufacture machinery which, in so far as its range of physical qualities, operational characteristics and efficiency are concerned, is reasonably equivalent to the machinery for which relief of duty is being sought.
e (5:10 p.m.)
Proven capability may be deemed as existing in Canada if: (a) the full range of technical and physical capabilities necessary for the production of the machinery for which remission is sought exists within the normal operational framework of at least one manufacturer; and (b) such facilities have in fact produced machinery which, in the judgment of the Board, has demonstrated a production competence reasonably equivalent to that required to produce the machinery for which remission is sought.
The criterion of public interest will be applied, in its broadest sense, in relation to the main objective of the machinery proposal, namely, that of encouraging the development of efficient Canadian industry. It is understood that in the main importations of machinery contribute to the maintenance, improvement and expansion of efficient industrial activity in Canada. In the typical case, therefore, remission of duty would be regarded as being in the public interest in cases where such machinery is not available from production in Canada. Such remission should assist manufacturers to be more competitive by reducing their capital costs. There may be instances, however, where the machinery and equipment advisory board finds final authority in granting remission.

December 12, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Drury firm are clearly inconsistent with the development of efficient Canadian industry. In such exceptional instances, the board may advise the minister that remission is not in the public interest.
Provision is being made for appeals from the findings of the machinery and equipment advisory board in respect of applications for remission of duty under tariff item 42700-1.
Appeals will be referred to a review board composed of three members from outside of government. Such a board will be established by the governor in council pursuant to the Department of Industry Act to deal with cases as and when they arise. The chairman would be selected because of the disinterested vantage point which his experience and position in the community would enable him to take, and the two other members may be drawn from those sectors of industry that are important users and manufacturers of machinery. The review board, like the advisory board, will be expected to take a practical rather than a legalistic view of cases coming before it.
When the machinery and equipment review board is of the opinion that remission should be granted in any case on which the advisory board had recommended to the contrary, the Minister of Industry would normally accept the review board's findings and recommend remission to the governor in council.
In any case where the review board supports an appeal that relief of duty should not have been granted, the advisory board will be guided by the review board's findings in respect of future applications for remission on the machinery in question. However, such an opinion could not be regarded as a firm precedent, since the facts about availability of machinery from production in Canada will be constantly changing.
At this point, I would like to comment on the market for machinery, and the characteristics of Canada's machinery industry.
The predominant feature of much of the industrial machinery and equipment market is that competition is international and severe. No industrial country can hope to produce its total machinery requirements. The range of products is too diverse and manufacturers in various countries have developed specialized products with which it is uneconomic to compete. In 1964, for example, the United States imported industrial machinery amounting to $900 million; U.K.- $1,015 billion; West Germany-$1 billion;

Japan-$595 million. All these figures are expressed in United States dollars.
Since competition tends to be international in character, it is important for a nation's machinery industry, particularly in an economy of Canada's size, to aim at manufacturing an increasingly selective range of machinery designed and priced to be competitive in both domestic and export markets. This achievement would help to offset, in our balance of trade, necessary imports of other machinery which cannot be manufactured domestically on an economic basis.
The basic characteristics of the Canadian machinery industry are that it is largely foreign owned, produces a wide range of products in relatively small volume, and is oriented toward the domestic market which has been protected by a relatively high tariff. In many cases, therefore, little product development is carried on, and economics of scale and specialization have not been achieved to any significant degree.
The fact that the Canadian machinery industry is largely foreign owned is at once its principal strength and weakness. The industry's diversity, know-how, and steady expansion since world war II are largely due to the initiative of foreign corporations which established subsidiaries to exploit the advantages arising from proximity to the market, a modest but long-standing tradition of excellence in the metal working industry, competitive wage scales, and tariff protection. However, the resulting orientation of production of parent designed machines toward the domestic market-since markets outside Canada have been largely supplied by the parent corporations or their other subsidiaries-has limited Canada's machinery exports, reduced opportunities for volume production, and discouraged the development of machines of unique design and performance. There are exceptions, of course, in respect of the extent of design and production engineering being carried on in Canada. These are principally in the field of heavy equipment for use in the resource and primary materials industries, as well as in harnessing electric power.
Part of the machinery industry is, I should add, Canadian owned. While the companies are modest in size, they have demonstrated a great deal of initiative both in design and marketing in the domestic and export market. Some of their achievements are quite remarkable.

If the development of the machinery industry is to be sustained, it must keep pace with advancing technology in a market which is becoming increasingly international in character. The overriding interest of machinery users in obtaining the most advanced capital equipment is compelling machinery builders in every country to take a critical look at both their manufacturing methods and their products to determine what improvements and research and development are required.
Fortunately, there are encouraging signs that Canadian machinery producers appreciate the necessity for adjusting to these circumstances, and are making various arrangements with their parent corporations to do so. These include moves toward greater specialization, broadening sales policies to include export markets, and expanding design engineering activity. Evidence of these trends to date includes the improved export performance of the industry in recent years, the decisions made by some parent corporations to assign responsibility to Canadian subsidiaries for the manufacture of particular products for international markets, and the industry's increasing participation in the Department of Industry's program for the advancement of industrial technology.
There is good reason for optimism about the future of the Canadian machinery industry. The requirements of our manufacturing and service industries for machinery in the general categories classifiable under tariff item 42700-1 are now about one and a quarter billion dollars per annum. The machinery producers' share of this market has been growing steadily and now amounts to almost
The Budget-Mr. Sherman half of the total. Further, some of these producers have shown that they can supply specialized products in world markets which are competitive both in respect of design and price. The Kennedy round will provide greatly improved opportunity for expansion along these lines.

I believe that the Canadian machinery industry should be able to cope with the competitive conditions which lie ahead and grow steadily provided, of course, it continues to display imagination and initiative, together with a willingness to adjust. I am confident that the machinery program will impart a strong thrust in the direction of higher productivity in the machinery industry, reduced costs in industry generally, and a better performance of the economy as a whole.
