speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this stage it is not my intention to try to make a major contribution to the budget debate. By this I mean a major contribution covering the whole spectrum of financial and fiscal problems confronting the country, which have been discussed by the minister the other evening and during the debate which has taken place over the past five or six days. At the same time, if my contribution is not major from the point of view of the spectrum it covers I hope it will not be unimportant because there is one specific and particular aspect of fiscal policy and financial affairs to which I want to devote myself and which I think demands some attention, requires some interrogation, and deserves some answers and illumination.
The basic message of the Conservative party with respect to the fiscal and financial affairs of the country, with respect to the economic crisis in which we are currently trapped and with respect to the minister's budget speech, has been clearly and carefully enunciated by the leader of this party and various other hon. members, including the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith), the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr), and several other hon. members who are highly qualified to discourse on this subject at some length and who have made important and compelling contributions to the debate. Anything I could add in the areas with which they have concerned themselves would probably be nothing more than an exercise in gilding the lily. So, Mr. Speaker, as I suggested a moment ago I am not going to
December 12, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Sherman attempt to cover the broad range and spectrum of fiscal and financial ills. The speakers to whom I have referred have done so in an eloquent and illuminating fashion. However, I do wish to place myself on record as agreeing with and subscribing to the general view of my party so far as the budget is concerned and so far as the financial and fiscal affairs of the nation are concerned.
At the present time there is a motion picture playing in movie houses in various Canadian cities. It is called "The Flim-Flam Man". I think its title can be applied most significantly, carefully and meaningfully to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) and his colleague the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson). The budget exercise of the past week must indeed be regarded as an exercise in flim-flam. If there is any flim-flam man operating in the nation at large at present it is the Minister of Finance, and if there is anyone assisting him in that exercise it is the Minister of National Revenue, for never in the life of this parliament, which now spans almost two years, have we seen such an exercise in flim-flam as the so-called budget that these two ministers have attempted to foist on this national legislature and on this nation.
The government's so-called savings program, as announced by the two ministers to whom I have referred, is certainly an exercise in flim-flam, double-talk and hypocrisy. No Canadian who has any experience or connection with the business and industrial community, any connection with the corner grocery store, any connection with the fundamental function of bringing up a family and running a household, is going to be fooled by the kind of semantics offered to this house when the budget was introduced and later offered by the Minister of National Revenue when he rose to attempt to defend, rationalize and explain what he described as a serious commitment to savings and to cut-backs in public expenditures.
As I have said, sir, there is really one specific area about which I want to talk, although there are a number to which I would like to devote some attention. Like other Canadians, those who live in my constituency, Winnipeg South, are still waiting for answers to questions dealing with the fiscal and financial area. They are still waiting for answers to legitimate, reasonable, sensible requests that have been advanced by this side of the house during the course of the past two years but which have so far fallen on deaf ears.

I speak of such requests as our suggestion for elimination of the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials, a tax which militates most severely against construction in cities like my own, Winnipeg. I speak of our request for some action in the area of the cost of living, the cost-price squeeze and the cost-price spiral which now hold hundreds of thousands, yes, millions of Canadian taxpayers, home owners and housewives in thrall, indeed in slavery. I speak of our request for some kind of relief, some kind of escape from the oppression currently being suffered by pensioners, in all categories, including superannuated civil servants, senior citizens and war veterans. The whole community of pensioners is a community in thrall, in slavery, existing in extreme difficulty if not absolutely suffering at the present time as a consequence of the run-away influences and pressures in this country, about which the government has done nothing during the two year life of this parliament.
We have also advanced a legitimate request for action in the area of income tax relief for small home owners in so far as the real estate taxes on their houses and properties are concerned. We have made the legitimate suggestion that real estate taxes on owner occupied homes should be deductible from taxable income for income tax purposes, at least up to a certain level of deduction.
These are among some of the suggestions we have made to prime the economy and restore the faith of the people in the financial affairs of this country, to inspire and generate the populace to a new pride in the jobs, professions and undertakings they carry out for Canada, and to create a new excitement about Canada. We have made these suggestions during the various budget debates in the two year life of this parliament and in the throne speech debates at the opening of both sessions of this parliament.
These are subjects to which I could devote the full time allotted to me under the rules during this debate but they are being covered by other speakers. All I want to do at this time with respect to such items is to mention them and again place on the record the fact that we on this side of the chamber, and I am personally speaking for my own constituency, urgently request the government to take a look at these items, among others. Let members of the government examine their books, hearts and consciences to see whether or not some of the difficulties, some of the enslavement in which Canadians

are currently trapped can be relieved if not totally removed by bold action, by improvisation, by experimentation, by leadership along the lines of the proposals we have made.

In moving from that section of my remarks to the nub of the speech I should like to make I reiterate again that we urge the government to remove the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials and to adopt and experiment with some of the suggestions which have come from this side of the house with regard to the cost of living. We urge the government to take action to remove the chains from the pensioners of this country in all categories. We urge the government to take a look at the substantial investment the small home owner has in this country and grant him some relief from income tax along the line of the realty tax deduction to which I referred a moment ago.
Having said that I wish to come to the specific item I should like to present to the Minister of Finance at this time, that is, the issue of the new 1967-68 series of Canada savings bonds. It seems to me that the whole history in respect of this bond issue is symptomatic of the manner in which this Liberal administration has mismanaged national financial affairs in Canada today.
The original idea in respect of Canada savings bonds was to develop and establish the savings habit on the part of ordinary Canadians. The original philosophy was that there should be an incentive to exercise thrift and good management among the average taxpayers, among ordinary Canadians like those who sit in this house and those at home who sent us here. At the time the savings bonds program was introduced in Canada there were relatively few vehicles available to the public which offered a secure savings medium that was convertible to cash on demand. There were not very many avenues to which an average wage earner could turn in order to find a good solid investment. Moreover, there were not many investments of this type which were immediately convertible to cash on demand in times of need. Therefore the savings bond vehicle filled a void in the life of the average Canadian in the context of his financial life. Philosophically it provided a valuable assist to the legislators and leaders of this country who, while devoting their attention to preparing more serious political issues, wished to encourage good, sound financial and monetary habits as much as they possibly could.
The Budget-Mr. Sherman
The philosophy of encouraging thrift and good management on the part of Canadians on every main street in every town and village was a highly laudable one. This, however, no longer is the case. There are now a great many institutions, vehicles and avenues through which the average Canadian can obtain every benefit which originally was available to him only through the savings bonds. Institutions such as trust companies, insurance companies, mortgage dealers, financial houses and mutual funds offer untold opportunities for the small Canadian to make an investment which will provide him a good rate of return and offer him immediate convertibility into cash if and when needed.
As I say, there are today many vehicles and avenues of this type because, as no one in this chamber would deny, times have changed. Times have changed financially, fiscally and socially. They have changed as much in this area as they have in any other area of Canadian life or in any other sector of the Canadian community. With the change of times apparently there has also come a change in government thinking in respect of savings bonds. As an illustration of this point one need look no further than the fact that whereas once the maximum amount an individual could hold in Canada savings bonds, war bonds, or whatever they were called in the original concept, was $5,000 the maximum has now been raised to $50,000.
There are not very many average wage earners in this country who have $50,000 to invest in Canada savings bonds or in any other investment. I doubt that this point would be seriously challenged in this chamber. So from this provision in respect of this series of bonds one can only draw the very obvious inference that the government no longer is seriously concerned about the original philosophy behind Canada savings bonds. What the government is now planning to do by means of Canada savings bonds is raise money to bail it out of trouble.
There are probably many Canadians who could invest $5,000 in Canada savings bonds and a few who might be able to stretch it to $10,000, but how many ordinary Canadians can invest $50,000? The only people who can invest $50,000 are the wealthy Canadians, the affluent investors, the capital money lenders, the people who deal in loans, bonds, investments and securities day in and day out every week. These people know the market, know the business and have the kind of money to invest in projects of this type.
December 12, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Sherman There is nothing wrong in changing the philosophy in respect of Canada savings bonds or in getting away from the philosophy of encouraging the average Canadian to invest by this method. There is nothing wrong with raising the ceiling to $50,000 with the intention of making these bonds available not only to the average Canadian but to the big money men, except the motive behind it. What is wrong with it is not the actual mathematical exercise itself but rather the motive behind it, that is, the motive or objective with regard to the 1967-68 series of Canada savings bonds of raising money for the federal treasury. The purpose is not to encourage the savings habit, as it once was, but to raise money for the federal treasury. That being the case, I suggest to every member of this house and to every person in this country that we have come to a sad day in the evolution of savings bond philosophy.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
The question arises automatically and instinctively, is this a sensible way for the government to raise money? The answer to that question is emphatically, unequivocally and unarguably no. It is not a sensible way for the government to raise money. It is a very expensive way for the government to raise money. Why does the government not go into the capital money markets to raise money, as has always been its traditional and acceptable practice? Let me tell you why. The government cannot get money in the capital money markets because there is no confidence in the government, particularly in respect of its bonds.
What has the government done under the guise of giving small Canadian investors and average Canadian home owners the opportunity to get in on the new series of savings bonds which pay pretty substantial rates of interest? This government has gone to the 20 million or 19,999,000 Canadians of average means and decided through this savings bond issue to bilk them of every dollar they can in order to bail themselves out of trouble. In so doing they have undertaken the most expensive exercise in money raising it would be possible for any government in Canada to undertake at this time. The corollary to the first question I asked-is this a sensible way to raise money-must be, is this the only way the government can raise money? Obviously the answer, sadly, reluctantly and regrettably, is yes. Otherwise the Minister of Finance would not undertake such a tortuously expensive method of raising money.


If the government had the confidence of the capital money markets and the people who deal in those markets and could get its money in the normal way, there would have been no flamboyant savings bond issue such as this series which pays an average yield of 5.48 per cent interest to maturity, with the bonds doubling in value if held for 13 years.
If this is the only way the government can raise money to bail itself out of trouble then, as I suggest, the government cannot command the confidence of the regular markets where it would normally go to raise the money it needed.
If what I suggest is so and I believe it to be so, the government should have the moral courage to tell us that this is the situation. Canadians have the stamina to take it and to face an economic crisis, but they like to know what the facts are. We have had enough of what I referred to earlier this afternoon as flim-flam. We want to know what the situation is. We will pull in our belts and fight this crisis as other nations have fought other crises in other times.
This is a hopeless exercise in hypocrisy, and I am referring to the government and the minister involved shirking their responsibility and asking us to stick our heads in the sand. The government is confusing us with overture, appeal and embellishment. What I have in mind is the advertising campaigns which were conducted in respect of the 196768 series of Canada savings bonds. We are being led down the garden path. The government is deluding us into thinking that everything is right and good and that in fact we can afford to issue a series of bonds with extremely attractive interest rates and extremely impractical results. If the Minister of Finance asks me why I think this is such an expensive way to raise money for the federal treasury I will consider it a privilege and a pleasure to tell him why.

This is the most expensive exercise possible in which the minister could indulge because of the cost connected with the issuing of a series of bonds of this type. I refer particularly to the commissions which are paid on these new bonds. We must also consider the extremely expensive cost of advertising, including full page advertisements in national, local and regional newspapers. These advertisements have even appeared in the weekly newspapers in this country from coast to coast. This is extremely costly. We must also consider the cost of
December 12, 1967

direct mail campaigns which include the distribution of pamphlets such as the one I hold in my hand. Various other advertising media have also been used to promote this bond issue. Of course this is salesmanship, and no one challenges the necessity for salesmanship. However, salesmanship for an unnecessary exercise is unnecessary.
^ In this case the exercise, as I suggested, stems and derives from motives and objectives which are wrong and involve an additional expense to this country which we at this time in our current economic and financial crisis can ill afford. There is an additional cost which I have not yet enunciated relating to the new issue of savings bonds. I refer to the new interest on the turnover versus the old interest. The new interest is to average 5.48 per cent if the bonds are held to maturity. As I suggested, the bonds will double in value if they are held for 13 years. The additional interest, the tremendous advertising costs and the commissions and the bank charges levied in the case of each new bond represent a staggering expense in respect of an exercise developed on the basis of incorrect reasoning; a wrong philosophy regarding savings bonds and an attempt to reach the average Canadian on the streets of this country in every town and village in order to pull the government out of the fiscal difficulty in which it now finds itself.
There is also the question of the risk involved in such a bond issue, and I hope the minister has considered the extreme hazard he shoulders in this regard. What would happen if, for example, the people of Canada should become more worried than they are and create a sudden run for cash in exchange for bonds? These bonds are negotiable at any time. What sort of predicament would the government find itself in then and what sort of financial state would Canada be m? Added to the mistaken philosophy, the disastrous concept, the wrong reason for undertaking this exercise to obtain capital in this risky way, and the exorbitant cost, is this additional risk which is an element in itself that increases the cost. I am sure, the result will be extremely disastrous for the people of Canada. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I go on record as condemning this exercise undertaken by the Minister of Finance and the government as an unwise and most expensive one for the nation at this time.

Someone said, "Good". I thought that would be the response. I will have to leave out the bouquets and perhaps some of the criticisms. I wish to make a few comments, however, with regard to the budget that has been introduced. Various factors, allegedly beyond the control of the government, have been blamed for the situation facing the country at the present time. But I think it is evident that the policies pursued by the government and its disregard of the effects of its borrowing and spending practices have been largely responsible for the problems that face us at this time.
The minister has now introduced a budget which calls for increased taxes and reduced borrowings. I should like to refer first of all to the proposal in regard to tax increases. Under the present system there are only two sources of money with which to pay government expenses, namely, taxes and borrowings. Just a few days ago my colleague the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) spoke about the tax increases and said, as recorded on page 5155 of Hansard:
Taking these costs-
The costs of government.
an<i applying them to the net national income of the Canadian people we find that 57 cents out of every dollar that is earned by Canadians is taken back by governments at one level or another. If we include the net cost of government, that cost which is financed through taxes and not through other sources of income, we find that nearly 50 per cent of every dollar that is earned by Canadians is taken back by government in the form of taxes to pay for the cost of government.
This indicates very clearly the extent to which the taxation structure of Canada is draining the resources of our people. We must consider the effect of rising costs occasioned by tax increases on the take-home pay of Canadians. Our workers are beginning to think that about all they have to do now is sign their cheques and send them to the government. The other evening I was listening to Professor Reuben Bellan, professor of political science at the Manitoba university, who pointed out that the tax increases are liable to increase the demands of workers for increased wages and this process will be carried on to the point where it affects the unemployment picture. Therefore we must consider the entire tax structure as it affects the cost of living. It has now reached the
December 12, 19G7

The Budget-Mr. Patterson point where it will be a case of diminishing returns if the tax load is increased any more.
However, we find that the government has conflicting policies. We discovered this in respect of the housing situation. The government stressed the importance of housing for our people, gave incentive bonuses for construction and then turned around and imposed the 11 per cent sales tax and cut off the bonuses. This was responsible for the raising of mortgage rates. So we find that in many ways the policies of the government are directly affecting the cost of living, and it now finds it must increase taxes in order to try to solve the problem.
An article that appeared in the Globe and Mail of November 16 last had as its heading, "Can Economy Take Tax Rise? Experts Wonder." The article pointed out that the need for higher taxes to bail Ottawa out of its financial troubles is generally accepted. The article then raised the question of whether the economy will stand a further tax hike.
I believe this is something that we and the government should take into consideration. We believe it will not be effective in solving the problems of inflation. In fact, an article which appeared in the Monetary Times of November, 1967, stated that a tax increase does nothing directly to contain the sort of inflation in which we find ourselves at the present time but instead it risks intensifying it.
We must consider the effect these measures will have on the employment picture. As has been stated, it seems that the government is embarking upon a plan to reduce employment. This will, of course, affect the welfare of Canadians all across the country. It has been said that the government is restricting its expenditures. We concur in the policy of the government with regard to curtailing the cost of government. This has been a source of great concern to the Canadian people for many years. I believe the time has come when this aspect of the problem must be seriously considered.
However, I believe that in outlining the ways in which this is to be effected the minister struck at some very vital areas which I believe should not have been included in the curtailing of expenditures. The question of superannuated civil servants has been raised. As a member of the committee set up to study this problem I, as well as every other member, was shocked to hear the statement that no increase in pensions will be forthcoming.

It has been said that we must reduce borrowings in order to take the pressure off the private capital market. I call attention to the fact that we have means by which this can be accomplished, but the government has acted very slowly. Even though it has moved slightly in this field, we believe that the Bank of Canada should be used to finance at least part of the government's expenditures in order that pressure may be taken off the private capital market, thereby releasing more money for the development of this country.
I would mention the reduction in the lending programs of the government. Here I point out that the government is dealing with very critical situations, for instance, national housing. I intended to deal at some length with this matter, Mr. Speaker, but time does not permit. I believe it is catastrophic that the government should reduce its contributions to the residential home construction program. There are several other factors in this regard but I do not have time to deal with them as my time has almost expired. I simply say that in the absence of adequate and effective monetary and fiscal policies designed to enable Canadians to provide for their immediate needs, they must mortgage their future to provide for the present.
The other evening I viewed the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith) on television. He said he doubted that the government would ever be upset because members to his extreme left would see to it that they were not in the house when votes were taken or they would lend their support to the government. I call attention to the fact that if all the members of his party had been present the other evening there would have been more than enough members to upset the government and put an end to the policies that are now in operation. Therefore I repudiate the implication that we must take the responsibility in this connection and I suggest to the hon. member for Perth that he should take a look at his own party.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) felt it necessary to attack me and describe me as the official hatchet man of the caucus and of the Liberal machine. This in itself does not particularly concern me, although I might add at the outset of my remarks this language is hardly the type of language that one would have expected from the Leader of the Opposition, who was supposed to introduce a new level of debate into the house. What does concern me, however, is the inference that I would use the cause of national unity as a part of political, partisan tactics.
If the Leader of the Opposition were in the house this evening, and I have adopted the usual courtesy of informing the hon. member that I was about to speak, I could assure him that I share his view about the necessity for caution when we are discussing issues that separate this country today. At the outset of my remarks, I want to assure the house that it is not my intention tonight to retaliate for what I consider to be an unfair and unwarranted reflection on my conduct as a member of the House of Commons. However I would not want the hon. member, if he were here this evening, to interpret the remarks I am about to make as an apology. Since reviewing my speech on Thursday night I am more convinced than ever before that no apology is indicated. I can only conclude, after rereading my
DEBATES	5339
The Budget-Mr. Mackasey remarks, that the hon. gentleman over-reacted to what he presumed I was about to say, rather than to anything which does appear in Hansard. Certainly the newspaper accounts of the furore indicate that the members of the press gallery were also puzzled as to what upset the hon. gentleman. The Montreal Star, in its issue of last Saturday, stated the following:
The normally cool and aloof Mr. Stanfield slashed into Mr. Mackasey with fangs suddenly bared. He ended up cutting himself.
Coming out of his parliamentary pensiveness for the first time, the new Conservative leader blew his cool on an imagined slight by Mr. Mackasey. Observers today are still wondering what he was angry about.
I want to assure the house and members of the opposition that had I implied that the Leader of the Opposition endorsed the Estates General, or had I said he endorsed their views or their findings, then I could understand the angry and rather violent reaction. If he drew from my remarks that I intended to accuse him or imply that he endorsed separatism, then I can assure him that this was not my intention. The Leader of the Opposition may be surprised to know that in the five years I have been participating in these debates, sometimes rather vigorously I will admit, I have never found it necessary to make my point by attacking the personality, language, religion, personal life or private life of any member of the House of Commons.
On the contrary, Mr. Speaker, I have tried, with some modest success, to be an instrument for national unity in this house and to bring about a better understanding of the problems of national unity amongst the members of the House of Commons. It is my intention to dwell on that subject in a few moments. Had time permitted me the other evening-and hon. members will recall I was cut off by the vote-I had intended to speak about the Estates General. I had intended to point out that I had supported the original concept of the Estates General, the idea of bringing together leaders from all the leading organizations existing in the French speaking communities in the province of Quebec, and outside of Quebec. I had encouraged friends in my riding to attend the recent meeting. I encouraged them in the naive belief that these friends, true representatives of my community, were believers in confederation as an instrument which, while not perfect had, as Claude Ryan recently points out in the Le Devoir, permitted complete freedom of religion, language and
December 12, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Mackasey assembly to all French speaking people in Quebec since 1867.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
I have as much right as the Leader of the Opposition to express an opinion in this house as to whether or not the Estates General acted in a serious manner in prejudging the issues. I presume they were assembled to discuss the issues in a democratic manner. To refuse to fly the Canadian flag did not seem to me a few weeks ago, nor does it seem to me now, an indication that serious men discussing a serious subject were doing so in an objective manner. This is essentially what I was about to say the other evening had time permitted. I repeat, I had no intention of implying by using the word "endorse" that the official opposition and its leader were endorsing the separatist conclusions of the Estates General. Certainly there were serious people present at the meeting, serious people not only from Quebec but from other communities outside Quebec, and it is regrettable that these serious people were not permitted to advance their arguments for confederation because of the atmosphere which prevailed at that meeting.
I might point out to the hon. gentleman if he were here tonight that as long ago as in 1964 I said in the house, and I gladly repeat now, that under the democratic system which prevails in our country Canadians have the right to endorse any philosophy they wish. They can support the cause of the Liberals, the Conservatives, the New Democrats, the Creditistes, the Social Crediters, or even separatism or communism. The presence in the House of Commons of the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) who has decided to adopt the philosophy of separatism is proof of this. I happen to believe that this is the right and privilege of the hon. member under the constitution of this country.
A close look at the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition as they appear at page 5066 of Hansard, as compared with mine which appear at page 5191, will indicate, as the Montreal Daily Star has already pointed out, that I made no attempt to twist the words of the hon. gentleman for political advantage.

When at the recent Montmorency conference the Conservatives accepted in principle the theory that two nations exist in Canada, at least in the cultural sense. I welcomed this. I welcomed it because it represented to me the existence of many enlightened people in that party who were willing to stand up and indicate their willingness to endorse the necessary changes in attitude that must come before true unity in this country becomes a reality.
I went further, Mr. Speaker, and I think the following extract from my remarks made on that day have particular significance because again they were made as a tribute to the party opposite. I said this:
Certainly it took more courage on the part of members representing constituencies in the west or in the maritimes to openly endorse this concept than on my part or the part of other members who represent ridings in the province of Quebec.
I submit that these are hardly the words of a petty partisan politician who would use the cause of national unity for political reasons.
I suggest, at the risk of upsetting the hon. gentleman were he here this evening-and I say this in true humility-that I have no lesson to take from him or anyone else in the

house when it comes to discussing the question of national unity in Canada. The Minister of Finance, as well as the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. Groos), made that point quite adequately when they took part in the debate on Friday.
I do not know what the Leader of the Opposition was saying about national unity in 1962, 1963 and 1964, and I do not know what legislation he was passing in Nova Scotia to help the minorities in that province, but I do know what I was saying both in and out of the house. It might be of interest to the hon. gentleman to know that during that period of time I had the opportunity to visit the excellent universities in his province and in the other maritime provinces. Certainly when I went to Nova Scotia I was well received there, and so was my message that tolerance and understanding should exist if Canada is to continue. The intention then, as it is today, was to point out to the country the fair and equitable treatment which I have received in the province of Quebec as one of the English speaking minority who was born in that beautiful province.
Time does not permit me to review all the speeches, or even a few of them, that I have made in the house on this subject, but I am sure the hon. gentleman, if he would take the trouble to look up my maiden speech made in the house in 1962, just a few days after I became a member of the House of Commons, would realize that five years ago I had no hesitation in speaking on this subject or in pointing to my own constituency as a perfect example and blueprint of what Canada in the future should be.
In 1963 I made some observations which may be of interest to the house, since they refer to the B and B commission, and which are set out at page 313 of Hansard of May 27, 1963. Before reading what I said, however, I might remind members of the house that four years ago bombs were exploding in the province of Quebec, and that, apart from Senator Lamontagne and myself, there were not too many people in the province of Quebec speaking against separatism or for the cause of federalism in that province. This is what I said at the time:
Rather than wait for the full implementation of the royal commission report, I think steps can be taken immediately to further the cause of bilingualism, at least in our senior civil service departments. I do not subscribe to the theory that all must be rectified by 1967. Certainly there is no magic date when all these differences of opinion must disappear. But I do think that confederation should at least mark the date of stocktaking, when

I think, Mr. Speaker, that every Canadian is duty bound to acquaint himself a little more with French Canada. Further in that speech, referring to the constitution and to the royal commission, I said the following:
I remain one of the optimists as far as the future of confederation is concerned.
I should have said "constitution" instead of "confederation". Then I went on to say:

However, I believe confederation must be reviewed and its contents more clearly defined. It is not by isolation that Quebec will fulfil its destiny. It is not by retiring from confederation that Quebecers will realize the fulfilment of their economic dreams. That hon. member's opinion, I understand, is highly valued and sought by the Leader of the Opposition. The hon. member for Queens said these words on that occasion-and this is his language: If it is flowery I ask hon. members to remember that we all have our own peculiar style.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to begin by congratulating the hon. member for Verdun on his wise, reasoned, reasonable, very sound and very eloquent remarks which he has addressed to a profoundly important subject.
The subject, if I may remind the house, was national unity.
In the manner of his delivery he demonstrated that he is indeed gifted, as are most Irish folk, with great felicity of phrase and it was a pleasure to hear him.

My good Irish friend across the way has the same charm. He does not use it as often as I try to use mine; that is our only difference. I continue:
I remember his leader, the Prime Minister,-

He was referring to the present Prime Minister.
-saying some months ago, when the hon. member for Three Rivers spoke eloquently in French on a similar subject,-
That hon. member was Mr. Balcer, as the house may recall.
-that the voice of moderation and reason must be heard in this house and in this country both in English and in French.
The hon. member for Queens continued:
I think today, Mr. Chairman, we have heard in English a most sound and valuable discourse on the subject to which we all must give our very best not only of attention but of effort.
Speaking on a serious note, Mr. Speaker, I should like to think that those words that were spoken by the hon. member for Queens over three years ago are still applicable to me today. If I ever thought that it was necessary for me to use the subject of national unity for political partisan purposes-and I hope that hon. members of the opposition will believe that I speak seriously-I should prefer not to be a member of the House of Commons.
I might also draw to the attention of hon. members of the opposition, and to the hon. member who is not here, the words that were spoken on my behalf by an honoured and respected member of the opposition, a former whip who now sits in the Ontario Legislature, the former member for Grey-Bruce, Mr. Winkler, who gave little quarter in debate and asked for none. He said, as reported on page 9497 of Hansard:
I am thinking also this evening of the words expressed by the hon. member for Verdun.... I think the hon. member for Verdun did a very commendable job this evening in presenting a sane, fundamental argument with regard to the problem that is before us. He did not over-emphasize it; he did not underscore it. He did not make it a sensational thing, he just brought the seriousness of it to the attention of the house. I feel that perhaps, in so far as this problem is concerned, this is the approach that we should take. I say again that I am pleased the hon. member for Verdun made that contribution this evening.

These are not words about national unity that were spoken yesterday, last week or three months ago. The remarks which I have quoted were made in the house three years ago.
I do not intend to quote the remarks of more members of the opposition, though it is tempting indeed to quote the present right
December 12, 1967

hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker), who felt no inhibition in congratulating me in this house for my contributions in debate. He is a member of the House of Commons, a House of Commons man, and he has often pointed out how mild is the language that we use in this house as compared with that used in what he refers to as the Mother of Parliaments.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I must point out something that has gone relatively unnoticed in the remarks that the hon. gentleman made on Friday. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, if the hon. gentleman seriously presumed from my remarks of Thursday evening that I was trying to attack him with the smear of separatism, that was not my intention. I say this and give my word as an hon. gentleman.
What puzzles me is his reference to the alleged fact that I made, not one attack on him, but two. The only other time I have mentioned the hon. gentleman has been during a debate on a supply motion, and if I recall that debate, the hon. gentleman seemed to be enjoying the mood of the house. I might ask him to look at the appropriate pages of Hansard. One can often tell the mood of the house by the humour of the interjections, including those of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill). I did not at that time intend to attack the hon. gentleman, nor did I attack him. If the hon. member feels, after reviewing the references that I made to him during the supply motion debate, which he seemed to enjoy, that my remarks constituted an attack on him, then I suggest it is time that he got acquainted with the level of debate in the House of Commons.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
There cannot be two sets of rules in this house, one for the hon. member and another for the rest of us. In conclusion I would say-and it is not too often that I pay tribute to my good friends in the far corner-that if any have been subject to my aggressiveness-call it that for want of a better word____
in the House of Commons, it has been the New Democratic party and its spokesman; and I may say that in all the years I have been here I have made them my special target, possibly because my philosophy is much closer to theirs than it is to the philosophy of hon. members directly opposite. But never once have they accused me of resorting to a personal attack as members of what I refer
The Budget-Mr. Hees
to as a gallant little band of misguided socialists.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We
are being presented at this time with what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) called an anti-inflationary budget. The hon. gentleman has told us that the economy has become "overheated" and must be "cooled off." You and I, Mr. Speaker, know that, in layman's language, this phrase simply means that the government has decided deliberately to create unemployment by withdrawing purchasing power from the taxpayers of this country, through the imposition of a 5 per cent extra tax on personal incomes.
Eighteen months ago the government introduced another anti-inflationary budget. At that time it imposed a 5 per cent refundable corporation tax. This was a fair anti-inflationary measure; it took 5 per cent of the profits which industry had accumulated during the year and, because the government felt there was a great deal to be feared from the spending of too much money in Canada at that time, it set aside the revenue derived from this tax, put it on ice, and promised to pay it back to the corporations within three years at a time when it considered that inflation did not pose a threat to the economy.
As I say, this was a fair anti-inflationary measure, and we know that the treasury will begin to pay back this tax to the corporations next June.
Today, however, in this so-called anti-inflationary budget, we are seeing the imposition of another 5 per cent tax, but this time it represents an increase in personal income tax levied on the people of this country-and it is no refundable tax; it will not be set aside, kept on ice, and paid back to the people when inflation is no longer a threat. No, this money will be spent by this government just as fast as it is paid in to the government's coffers. This tax is not anti-inflationary. On the contrary I intend to show that it is very much an inflationary tax. And it is a tax

December 12, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Hees
which is being demanded by this government because this administration has overspent drastically during the last four years; it finds itself today in a desperate financial situation, and this burden is being imposed on the Canadian people because hon. gentlemen opposite do not want to be forced to go to the bond market once again in the very near future. This money is being taken from the Canadian people in order to pay for government overspending. The tax we are considering is no more an anti-inflationary measure than I am. It is a measure to helieve the Minister of Finance and his colleagues, because they are under serious financial stress.
This tax is an inflationary tax. You and I know perfectly well, Mr. Speaker, that from this point on as soon as the unions begin to make their demands to the corporations for which they work, the amount of this tax will be included in their claims, in addition to anything else they expect to receive. As a result, this tax increase will be added to the cost of production, like any other cost, and passed on to the consumer, and it will raise prices to that extent. This 5 per cent tax is an inflationary measure, and this budget is not an anti-inflationary budget; it is an inflationary budget.
The government tells us we are being taxed because we have been overspending. Let us examine just what the government itself has been doing in this regard. What has been its record in connection with the spending of the taxpayers' money? In the last budget which the Conservative government presented, the budget of 1962-63, the country, through its government, spent $6,570 million. In the budget presented for the present fiscal year, 1967-68, we shall spend at least $9,646 million. Thus, in the four years during which this government has been in office, government expenditure has been increased by more than $3,000 million, or 47 per cent. And to show that they have not lost any of their skill in overspending, figures for the first seven months of the year, the latest period for which information is available, show that the increase in government expenditure amounts to 15 per cent. This illustrates the extent to which a government which is lecturing us on overspending is itself overspending, and thereby has created a situation, from which it hopes to extricate itself by the tax measures imposed on the people, as set out in the budget of a few days ago.
The government claims, through its Minister of Finance, that it intends to do a great deal in the way of cutting expenditure. We
[Mr. Hees.l
were told it intends to set an example by cutting down expenditures, both in the present budget for 1967-68, which does not expire until March 31 of next year, and in next year's budget as well.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
On November 2 of this year, Mr. Speaker, as noted on page 3775 of Hansard, I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) the following question:
I have a question for the Minister of Finance. In view of the minister's letter to the provincial treasurers, tabled in this house yesterday, in which he said-
I quoted the words in his own letter.
"We in the federal government have already re-assessed the spending programs and the lending operations of government departments and agencies-*"
Note these words, Mr. Speaker.
"-for the balance of the current fiscal year and for next year."
Then I went on to ask:
Will the minister advise the house when he intends to announce the reductions in expenditures for the present fiscal year which are to result from the re-assessment he has made?
The Minister of Finance replied as follows:
As I have said on a number of occasions, it is my intention to do so shortly.
In other words at that time, Mr. Speaker, he said that shortly he would outline not only the expenditures which they intended to cut in the budget of 1968-69 but also in the present budget of 1967-68.
Two weeks later I asked him in this house when he intended to make this announcement, and again he said he would do so shortly. Then, Mr. Speaker, we had him deliver his now famous budget message and I, like all other members, sat in this house and listened to hear him specify the cuts which he intended to make in the present budget, the cuts which he had said in this house he intended to make and that he would outline in the house for members to hear. I listened to that budget and, as we all know, he did not mention one single cut he intended to make.
The next day in the House of Commons I asked the minister whether, in view of the fact that he had assured us he would make this announcement and give us this information, he would give it to us then. His reply was that his colleague, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson), who is also the President of the Treasury Board, would
December 12, 1967

be outlining these cuts in detail when he made his speech in the budget debate.
So, Mr. Speaker, we listened with great interest to the speech which the President of the Treasury Board made in this house a few days ago. I listened to it. All members listened to it. Did we hear that minister mention one single reduction which he intended to make in the present year's budget, as had been promised to us by the Minister of Finance? No, Mr. Speaker, we did not. He did not mention the budget of 1967-68.
I have his speech here in my hand, because I could not believe my ears. I thought I must have missed something. I read his speech, page by page, line by line. There was not a single mention of anything in his speech dealing with the budget of 1967-68, the budget in the expenditures of which the Minister of Finance had assured the provincial treasurers, and had assured this house that he intended to make substantial reductions.
Mr. Speaker, this government is developing the same kind of thing from which President Johnson is suffering in the United States. It is beginning to suffer from a credibility gap. We are getting to a point where we cannot believe the word of ministers who stand up and state one thing and obviously do not mean what they say.
I had a similar experience a few days ago with the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand). I asked him a question regarding a speech he had made in Toronto to the Liberal association in Spadina riding, in which he was reported as saying that the reason the manpower training program had been held up was because of lack of action on the part of the provincial governments. I asked him, in view of what he had said in that speech, just which provincial governments had held up this program, and in what way? In a very haughty manner he stood up and said he had announced this in detail a few days previously in the house. I did not hear him on that previous occasion, and so I phoned his office. I asked them to send me a copy of the issue of Hansard, marking the statement in the speech which he had told me he had made in the house, so that I could check it. His office sent me the issue of Hansard. They marked the page very carefully but, Mr. Speaker, there was not one word dealing with what the minister told me he had said in this house-not one word; and this was his own department which sent me Hansard, and his officials had done the marking.
The Budget-Mr. Hees
We are getting to a point where we are not only getting rotten government from this government but we are getting statements we cannot believe, because they say things that are not true. These two ministers have told me definitely on various occasions that certain things were so, and on checking I have found they were not so.
There is a definite credibility gap developing on the part of this government, and that is a very serious thing indeed. Always up to now-and I have been in this house for 17 years, during which time I have sat opposite governments and I have been a member of governments-I have always been able to believe what ministers of the crown said on the floor of this house to members of parliament. Now we are getting to a point where we cannot believe what members of this government say. It is one thing to get inefficient, rotten government, but it is another thing to have this house misled, and I believe it has been deliberately misled by the two ministers I have spoken about this evening.
The President of the Treasury Board made a great many claims about what he considered to be great savings that he would be making in the 1968-69 budget, the budget which will be brought down next spring. Mr. Speaker, when you have been around here for a while, particularly if you have been a member of government and know the procedure that goes on every year when ministers submit their estimates to Treasury Board, you can understand what a farcical, ludicrous and fantastically amusing statement this public relations document I hold in my hand is, one which was probably produced by the public relations firm hired by the Department of Finance to function at public expense.
Anybody who has been a minister in a government knows perfectly well that every department every year-and this has gone on ever since parliaments began, and I am sure will go on as long as parliaments exist- brings before Treasury Board a list of everything-and I mean everything-that the departmental ministers would like to do for the good of the country, the good of the people of Canada. And these things are good things. A lot of them cost a great deal of money, but in the mind of a department and of the minister in charge of it they are good things and desirable things.
But, Mr. Speaker, they can only be introduced as part of a system of priorities. It is the job of the Treasury Board to decide what those priorities are. Every year any minister

December 12, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Hees
who has ever gone before Treasury Board has had ten, twenty, thirty, forty or fifty millions of dollars worth of possible expenditures lopped from his estimates, simply because the Minister of Finance, and through him the President of the Treasury Board, have decided that the government cannot afford to do these things at that time.
Every minister knows that a cabinet meets well before the budget is prepared. They decide what can be the total expenditure allowed, in view of the financial situation of the country at that time. The Minister of Finance then allots a certain over-all figure to each department, and they cut their coats according to the cloth available. Any good minister of finance cuts his series of coats to the cloth that is available to the government. That has always been done.
I would say, certainly while I have been here, that under Mr. Abbott, Mr. Harris, Mr. Fleming and Mr. Nowlan-those four ministers of finance anyway, and I am sure the ones before them-made the kind of cuts this government is making in the 1968-69 estimates, or cuts very close to them. But the reason these seem so fantastic to this government is obviously that the presidents of the Treasury Board in the past four years have simply not been able to bring themselves to cut expenditures down to what the country could afford to pay at that time. They have not been able to say, "Certainly they are things that are very desirable, but they must wait until we have the money to pay for them." As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, these Treasury Board ministers, these finance ministers seem to me to be very much the same sort of people as that very charming character, the girl who played the part of Ado Annie in the famous musical "Oklahoma," and sang the charming song entitled "I'm just a Girl Who Can't Say No." That is what they are; they are Ado Annies; they can't say no. The first time they are forced to say no they become so excited about it that they obtain a public relations firm to write a great speech saying that what they are doing is something new, whereas it is only something which has been done by every conscientious finance minister who ever held office in this country.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us have a look at the part this government has played in creating the inflation we are being taxed for today. As anyone in business knows, late in 1964 there appeared in this country a very

marked shortage of skilled workers. That shortage of skilled workers became more acute because this government did not have the foresight to enlarge sufficiently the facilities we introduced in 1961-62. These facilities are to train additional skilled workers to enable our factories, as we move into the automation period, to have the skilled workers they require to keep the factories producing. This government also did not, by means of immigration, bring in additional skilled workers to fill the gap. For that reason we were short of skilled workers. Therefore our factories could not produce up to the demand for goods which the affluent society required, and prices started to rise abnormally.
Mr. Speaker, you and I know that inflation is caused when too much money chases too few goods. There are two ways to cure inflation. The first is to reduce the amount of money available to chase the too few goods, but the positive way is to increase the supply of goods available for the money to chase. I am sure you, Mr. Speaker, because you are a very knowledgeable gentleman and I, would expect this government to adopt the negative method they have adopted. They reduced the amount of money available to buy the goods. They imposed a tight money policy upon this country. This tight money policy made it impossible for producers to enlarge their plant and purchase more equipment, whether they are on the farm, in a factory, in a store or wherever it might be. They could not buy the additional machinery and expand their plant so that they would be in a position to keep up with the demand for their goods. So, once again, prices began to rise abnormally.
Inflation began to take hold in a very serious way in this country. Because this government would not increase the training facilities sufficiently and would not bring in sufficient people through the immigration stream to fill the need for skilled workers, they imposed a tight money policy and inflation steadily increased in this country.
Then we move along to June of 1966. We find that the government stepped in with regard to three labour disputes, and imposed its will. The three labour disputes of which I speak are the wildcat strike of the dock workers of Montreal, and the threatened strikes on the seaway and in the C.B.C. The government intervened and imposed a 30 per cent wage increase in each case. This accomplished two things:	First, these wage
increases greatly affected all wage settlements that were made later. It is a well known fact that, at the time, the railway
December 12, 1967



workers were in the process of negotiation, and were ready to sign an agreement involving a 19 per cent wage increase. However, when they heard of the 30 per cent increase which the government had given the dock workers, they decided that 19 per cent was not enough. Eventually as you and I know, Mr. Speaker, they were awarded a 24 per cent increase.
Second, because of the government's intervention in the case of the dock workers' strike, by dealing with those who were engaged in an illegal work stoppage they made a wildcat strike legal. This government did not impose any penalty on the members of the union for going out on a wildcat strike. In fact they awarded them a 30 per cent wage increase. Therefore in addition to causing wage demands to be greatly accelerated, which has resulted in the fact that this year, for instance, wage increases in this country have averaged 8.7 per cent compared to 4.4 per cent in the United States- and you cannot compete with your greatest competitor if your wage increases are double his-this government, by stepping in and dealing with a wildcat strike and thereby making it legal, has greatly weakened the influence of good labour leaders who conscientiously try to stop their union members going out on a wildcat strike, or asking for wage increases which are not justified by increased productivity. Once again by these actions this government has increased inflation.
One of the costs of production is the cost of money. If the people of the country have confidence in the government, then the government is able to borrow money at reasonable rates of interest; if not, the rate goes up. The people of this country have lost confidence in the ability of this government to handle its financial affairs. They also know that probably every few months the government will find it necessary to go to the bond market again to ask for more money. So, because of the lack of confidence they have in the government, and because of the fact that the people of Canada know the government will come more and more frequently to the market for money, they have held off time and again, in the knowledge that if they hold off they will receive a higher rate of interest on the money they lend. This is what has caused the cost of money to rise to such a high degree that in this country we have at the moment the highest rate of interest in history, and bonds are at their lowest prices in 40 years. Since interest rates, and hence
The Budget-Mr. Hees
costs, steadily rise, inflation continues to rise also.
So we see that this government, which is taxing the people of Canada for inflation, is largely to blame for that inflation and, for the following reasons: First, they neglected to expand the manpower training facilities sufficiently to provide enough skilled workers so that our producers would be able to expand their production to meet the demand. Second, they imposed a tight money policy on the country, which has made it impossible for producers to expand their plant and equipment sufficiently to meet the increased demand for their products. Third, by intervening in labour disputes, and imposing 30 per cent wage settlements, they set an example which caused wages in Canada to increase at a rate of 8.7 per cent during the past year, compared to 4.4 per cent in the United States. Fourth, by rewarding a union which was out on a wildcat strike with a 30 per cent wage increase, they have undermined the influence of conscientious union leaders who attempt to restrain their members from going out on a wildcat strike, or demanding increases in wages which are not justified by increased productivity. The fifth reason that the government is to blame for this inflation is that by increasing government expenditures nearly 50 per cent during the past four years, and creating excessive demands on the bond market, they have caused the cost of borrowing to reach the highest level in history.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
You and I know, Mr. Speaker, that prosperity depends on the ability of a country to sell its goods in competition at home and on the export market. If costs rise abnormally, then selling prices will also rise abnormally. I have outlined in detail what this government has done to make costs rise and therefore to make selling prices rise.
As we know, the Kennedy round of tariff negotiations will come into effect on January 1 next. For that reason, competition here in Canada will become very much more difficult in the months ahead. Competition will also become more difficult because of the devaluation of the pound in Great Britain. Because of that devaluation, Canadian goods will be 15 per cent more expensive on the British market and British goods will be 15 per cent less expensive in Canada. These will be very important factors in our trading patterns in months ahead.
December 12, 1967

The Budget-Mr. J. R. Tremblay
Unemployment in this country in the past 12 months has already increased by 20 per cent, and by some 14 per cent during the last tour weeks for which figures are available. Freight carloadings, which represent a very accurate measure of the prosperity of a country, are down 6 per cent during the past 12 months. If we do not increase productivity very materially and very soon, and if we do not keep taxes from rising, and if this government does not control its spending, we will face exactly the same situation which caused the economic crisis in Great Britain a few weeks ago.
This government at this time appears to be singularly incapable of meeting the demands made upon it to do two things, to give leadership, and to solve problems which are becoming-

speechtext:
I thank you very much, Mr. Speaker, and hon. members of the house, for the courtesy of allowing me an additional two minutes to conclude my remarks.
Let us have a look at the future. What do we see? We see another increase in taxes in the spring to pay for medicare. Based upon the record of this government we will have an additional increase in taxes to cover the cost of this government indulging in increased spending. If taxes are increased they will be passed on to the people in the way of increased prices of goods. This is inevitable because labour demands higher wages to offset tax increases. We all know that commodity or corporation taxes are immediately passed on to the people in the form of higher prices. In the future we can see nothing but a very difficult situation developing.
Now is the time when all Canadians are looking to the government to give leadership in order to maintain economic health, productivity and employment. We do not seem
[Mr. Hees.}
to be obtaining this. All I can say in conclusion is that this government has become a tremendous disappointment to this country. All one can say for this government is that it has at least become a great social asset. Just before the Christmas holiday, we all gather together at this time in celebration of this festive season.
At the various gatherings which take place during this time one has only to mention this government to get people laughing. Those who do not laugh burst out crying. In any event one can get action in this way.
Let me suggest to the government that it should use the opportunity to provide leadership to meet the needs of these difficult times. If the government cannot do this it should get out of the way to allow some others to take over who can provide this leadership.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you very much for this opportunity to express my views on this matter. I am very grateful to those who are responsible for allowing me to sit in this house, and make my modest attempt to enumerate some points. I shall first set out my views regarding the wisdom of our fine Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp). Following that I shall make some observations about the speeches of hon. members opposite; and finally I shall offer a few comments about the crucial matter of constitutional affairs.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to call the attention of the house to the negative criticism aimed at the constructive and honest labour of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp).
It is not necessary to be a veteran in politics to realize that the remarks of my colleagues opposite are filled with superficial arguments, and I suggest that such remarks which sometimes unduly waste the time of the house constitute a perfect sample of political electioneering.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) even tried to project his image to the Canadian people with statements that have likely missed their mark. Last Thursday, he tried to impress his own gallery, that is 46 hon. members, or half his manpower and, between us, Mr. Speaker, it was not very gallant.
The hon. member for Colchester-Hants will not bear a grudge if I remind him of the calm, affable but firmly determined
December 12, 1967

tone of voice in which the Minister of Finance stated his case.
Those wise positions taken by the great accountant of the government have naturally carried back my hon. colleague to a quite recent past, when he was responsible for the budget of a province which, by the way, I find more attractive, especially since the arrival of my hon. friend in this house.
He may have relived some tense moments he had already experienced, and this is the reason for the weakness of his arguments and his ability to elude questions, in order to cheer up his partisans a little.
His financial critic had to resort to traditional expressions, to hackneyed phrases of political gatherings in order to give an appearance of justification to a non-confidence motion that he would not have submitted to the house had he entertained the least doubt about being able to defeat the government.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people no longer fall for that type of game. They are concerned with adopting a mature attitude and assuming their responsibilities, in stride with their government, to reach a common objective: a balanced national budget in the context of a progressive and deflationary economy.
My colleague for York South (Mr. Lewis), whose office is one of the best equipped in Toronto, took it upon himself, in a speech made last Wednesday, to request the cancellation of our defence programs. I quote his words, as they appear on page 5126 of Hansard for December 6, 1967:
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)

I suggest, as my leader suggested on November 20 in this house-
This is the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) who is speaking, of course.
-that we should postpone the construction of the two support ships and drop the purchase of the CF-5 aircraft. If all these things were cut out we would avoid unnecessary expenditures in the large amount of $500 to $000 million. I do not wish to go into the details of this now, because there will be other opportunities to do that.
and so on.

Once again, the serious nature of such a suggestion may be rightly questioned, as my hon. friend is well aware of what those cuts may entail; indeed, he knows it very well, if only through his affinities with labour
The Budget-Mr. J. R. Tremblay unions. He knows the tragic consequences for thousands of Canadian families that may ensue from the postponement of those defence production programs. Only in my riding, the result would be disastrous for at least 3,000 workers, not including the subsequent slow-down of our regional economy. As it happens, the same effects would be felt in the constituency of Levis.
Now, let us multiply those consequences by the actual number of naval yards in our country, and we will realize the shocking number of workers who would be made jobless through such an irresponsible action. I suggest that this attitude of the hon. member for York South concerning the welfare of the workers of our shipyards and aircraft plants denotes a lack of concern for the working classes.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to draw a psychological parallel between the hon. member for York South and the leader of the sovereignty movement in Quebec, who also referred to national defence but in other words, of course, and with a lot of television publicity. In fact, a complete crew of C.B.C. technicians and reporters all last week followed in Seven Islands, in the riding of Saguenay, this idol with clay feet who described as a "damn foolishness" the maintenance of military personnel who, as he said, "drag around Europe".
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, his favourite expression, when referring to the members of the armed forces, is:	"Social welfare in
uniform".
Mr. Speaker, I take advantage of this intervention to rise before the Canadian people in order to protest against such a flagrant lack of respect toward those who have served and who now serve in the Canadian armed forces. I protest indignantly against this attitude on behalf of the families of those who gave their lives to defend our civilization and on behalf of the thousands of workers who make a living by working in aircraft plants, in defence production plants and in shipyards all over the country.
Let us be serious and let us learn to be opportunists without endangering the livelihood of our citizens and without insulting the Canadian people. Drastic measures which are applied equitably, such as the ones advocated by the hon. Minister of Finance, are acceptable in view of what is at stake.
In my humble opinion, after having read everything I could on the subject, I notice that only demagogues and politicians who
5350	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. J. R. Tremblay subsist on "electoralism" manage to throw discredit on the fiscal policy presented in the house.
It goes without saying that Canadians as a whole are fully aware of an inflationary trend which is caused, as everyone knows, by an excessive increase in expenditures compared with the increase in productivity and revenues. This inevitable cycle is the price we have to pay for a prosperity which is sometimes self-suggestive and which prompts us too often-if I may jest about that-to put a grand piano and velvet drapes in a log cabin. The American giant which casts its shadow over us can probably afford luxuries which we have to do without.
Mr. Speaker, which one of us can accuse the other of being directly responsible for this rather alarming situation, in view of our high standard of living. I humbly submit that the present circumstances must incite us to choose rather than endure those disciplinary measures, and here is what the Minister of National Revenue and President of the Treasury Board said.
My remarks are in a vein similar to that of a large company which must from time to time review its administrative policies and its fiscal activities. This review of priorities and the adjustment of expenditures are made from a budgetary angle which invites us to live within our revenue. Radical decisions are called for to ensure continued progress. We must seize the opportunities which we have in the future and invest more in these, while cutting things which appear less important.
Mr. Speaker, we should greet the words of the minister in a spirit of elementary philosophy and practical sense.
A short review of the achievements of the government reveals a remarkable improvement in the Canadian living standard: the national pension plan, the old age assistance program, additional pension for old age security, student allowances, increased aid to the universities, manpower mobility, manpower retraining, subsidies to stimulate industry, water pollution control and countless other measures to improve the standard of living of Canadian citizens and to give them the second highest standard of living in the world.
Practical measures of national import such as the Canadian flag, the Centennial, Expo '67, Man and his World that has revealed to the whole world the capacity of our people, of a strong and dynamic nation.
Mr. Speaker, in such a brief analysis in the context of a fiscal adjustment, there is, naturally, a place for emotional considerations,

DEBATES	December 12, 1967
but reason argues for objectivity, practical sense and moderation and that is what I am striving for when I think of the recommendations of the report on bilingualism and biculturalism in Canada.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Recently, the hon. Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) stated that:
The independence of peoples prevails over the independence of states.
This is a resounding statement which describes perfectly the present reality. If a man like the Minister of Manpower and Immigration-"a prolific honourable man", as he was described by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge)-if this French Canadian, who has devoted twenty years of his life to promote the welfare of Quebec workers, is able to be optimistic with respect to the application of these recommendations of the royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism-frankly, they are worth much more than those of the separatists and the "sovereignists"-I do not hesitate in saying that, as a Canadian citizen, I want to flourish and prosper with my family and my fellow Canadians in a bicultural and, above all, an economically sound Canada.
The premier of Quebec himself, when he was leader of the opposition, congratulated the federal government about its decision to set up the Laurendeau-Dunton commission. Today, he is in authority and he states that this report might bring about agreements with Ottawa. The same day the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) said that this report would be discussed at the federal-provincial conference in January 1968. What more concrete plan could we ask for to work toward the unification of Canada?
Mr. Speaker, the constitutional climate is improving, needless to say. We are seeing at last the first rays of hope which are the antithesis to the pessimistic utterances of those who want to give Quebec to the United States at any cost, because it is well known that the gist of their separation or sovereignty thesis is to advocate the isolation of a province while serving an ultimatum on the rest of the country.
I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that Canadians look to that formula to achieve the unity of the nation. Fortunately for this house, the Laurendeau-Dunton report was tabled only after the election of the new leader of the loyal opposition. Now, we know, alas, how
December 12, 1967

the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Dief-enbaker) feels about the subject. On the contrary, and this is all to his credit, the hon. member for Colchester-Hants, his successor expressed very positive opinions, as did also the hon. members for Burnaby-Coquitlam and Villeneuve (Messrs. Douglas and Caouette). With regard to the hon. representative for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson), he expressed his assent, while making a few reservations, when the report was tabled. Those almost unanimous feelings, justify the hope that serenity will reign at the meetings on the orientation to be given the destiny of our country.
My most sincere wish is that the Lauren-deau-Dunton report will make English speaking Canadians aware of the Quebec fact, how it wants to become resolutely integrated with its language, its culture and its economy, to the rest of Canada, and take an active part in our national decision-making bodies.
Yes, I am an optimist. As a Canadian from Quebec, I am used to concessions, on the cultural level; I am willing to make that ultimate attempt. I will do my utmost with my limited means to help the cause of Canada, but I am convinced that the great task now rests on the good will and the courage of my English speaking fellow citizens.
Are bilingualism and biculturalism Canada's last chance? I should hope not, Mr. Speaker, because if that constitutional question is not reasonably and equitably settled, our Quebec will be taken over by you know who and, eventually, the giant who holds that $10 billion mortgage in our country will only have to cross the border to recover his property, or else.
Mr. Speaker, those perspectives will never materialize, I hope, and I should like to conclude my remarks by stating my confidence in our parliament, our government, our Canadian people and the courageous people in my riding who conscientiously toil in progressive industries within a favourable and beneficial economic framework from which they do not want to be divorced. Therefore, I am repaying them today this loyalty with which they have chosen to honour me.
