The remark that was just made from across the floor is an indication of what hon. members on the other side of the house think about the people in Nova Scotia, and the plight they face. I think the hon. member should rise and apologize, not to me because I can take it, but certainly to the people of Cape Breton. First and foremost he should apologize to the Prime Minister and to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who have shown the same concern for people in that province as I and other members on this side of the house have shown.
Why did I choose to direct my remarks to the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development, as well as to those ministers who are not here this evening? I also regret the absence of the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) because I should like to get to the bottom of certain statements which he made in the house not long ago in answer to a question with regard to the Sydney steel problem. He said at that time-and hon. members can look it up for themselves this time-that it would be ridiculous and silly for the government to plan a phasing out of the Sydney steel operation. At the same time the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development, when
December 12, 1867

he was out in Banff, spoke of government plans to phase out the Sydney steel operation. I ask the ministers who are present here tonight to convince their cabinet colleagues of the necessity for an absolute assurance that in the negotiations with the provincial government they will pay close attention to the plight of the Sydney steel industry. I also ask them to distinguish between Dominion Coal and Dosco, because at the time of the establishment of the Cape Breton Development Corporation the Prime Minister advised the house and the people of Nova Scotia, inadvertently I admit, that the Cape Breton Development Corporation would take upon itself the problem of dealing with the Sydney steel problem. When the matter was finally sorted out a denial of the previous statement was made. However, at that particular time the impression was left that the Cape Breton Development Corporation would look after this particular problem.
I should also like to ask the government to deal with Dominion Coal and the Sydney steel plant as two separate problems, regardless of the fact that Sydney is located within a 20 mile radius of Dosco. It was decided last spring that these two matters would be treated separately and would be looked upon as altogether separate questions. I trust the government will keep them separated and will deal with the Sydney steel problem as a separate problem entirely. I am sure this would be the approach, were Sydney located a couple of hundred miles away from the coal area. In any case these are two separate problems and I ask the government to consider them as such.
Not too long ago the people of Cape Breton demonstrated their concern in a manner which cannot be considered as simply one of crowd gathering, when in that area over 20,000 people organized what was called "the march of concern". The people who organized this march deserve to be congratulated. The behaviour of the crowd was excellent. Courtesy was shown throughout to the guest speakers, including the cabinet minister from Cape Breton.
I ask the government to show consideration for the people who are faced with this problem. I would further ask it to review the remarks made at that time by the federal representative, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who said: "We are searching desperately for a way to assist". On other occasions the minister remarked that this assistance may be extended through the Cape Breton Development Corporation.

The Budget-Mr. D. Maclnnis
Although I do not wish to anticipate the results of the negotiations between the government of Nova Scotia and the federal government, I trust they will be successful. I understand that before Premier Smith returns to the province he will discuss this matter with the Prime Minister, and it is to be hoped that the federal government will wish to grant assistance and, if necessary, place Sydney steel under the protection of the Cape Breton Development Corporation, thus enabling them to continue this industry.
Why should the industry be continued? There are many reasons, and I do not propose to take the time of the house tonight to elaborate on them. However, I should like the members of the government to compare the appeals and the statements made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare on behalf of the federal government, when he said that the government is searching desperately for a way to help and that assistance would be forthcoming through the Cape Breton Development Corporation, with the remarks made by the leader of the Liberal party in Nova Scotia during the recent legislative meeting there. The leader of the Liberal party in Nova Scotia had many criticisms, to offer at that time, and he left the impression, which I hope will be ignored by the federal government, that the Nova Scotia government has been taken in by Dosco. He listed a number of savings which Dosco has made as a result of the takeover of the company by the Nova Scotia government. He tried to impress upon the people of Nova Scotia that the action of the government of that province has resulted in savings for Dosco. He has completely missed the point. I trust that no one in the federal cabinet will consider that Mr. Regan, the leader of the Liberal party in Nova Scotia, knows anything about this problem. He has failed to recognize the fact that this was an emergency situation and that there would be many steel workers walking the streets of Cape Breton during the closing down of the Dosco steel operation.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
As I said, in listing the savings with respect to Dosco and in listing other figures, he failed miserably to mention that the takeover by the government of Nova Scotia has saved the federal government considerable sums of money with respect to unemployment insurance. He overlooked that. Instead he chose to talk about patronage.
December 12, 1967

The Budget-Mr. D. Maclnnis Here is a matter that is vital to the economy of Nova Scotia, Cape Breton and Canada.
It has been said before that if something is good for Canada, it is good for Nova Scotia; and if it is good for Nova Scotia, it is bound to be good for Canada. Yet the minister talked of patronage. He failed to note that this same government of Nova Scotia has recommended, for high office with the Cape Breton Development Corporation, a former president of the Nova Scotia Liberal Association. That is an obvious indication that the government of Nova Scotia is concerned only with the development and carrying on of that corporation. The minister failed to mention the fact that the former president of the Liberal association in Nova Scotia, Mr. Regan, had been recommended to the board of the Cape Breton Development Corporation.
I could list many reasons why this government should go all out in completely renovating the Sydney steel operation, in order to make it a viable industry. In that renovation the federal government in co-operation with the government of Nova Scotia, should make money available to that industry. It is not fair to expect the provincial government alone to carry this load. The fact that the government of Nova Scotia has moved so quickly in this matter and has avoided the complete shut down of the plant is an indication of its concern for the welfare of the people of this industry and of Cape Breton.
Some false impressions have been left about the aid which has been given to Cape Breton. Granted, without the subventions paid on coal over the last 38 years, our coal could not have reached its markets. Without federal aid the coal industry no doubt would have been dead long ago. Certain important steps have been taken by the Cape Breton Development Corporation, and it is hoped that there will be a future for our coal. This depends of course, on whether the necessary financial assistance is available.
I regret that a false impression has been created with respect to aid to Cape Breton. I think, judging from the representations that I have heard in this house, that members of the N.D.P. support the complete take-over by this government of the Sydney steel operation.

speechtext:
Yet, for some strange reason, some members of this house are trying to leave the impression


that Cape Breton depends entirely on government handouts. To illustrate what I mean, let me draw the attention of the house to a question that the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Saltsman) not long ago placed on the order paper. He wanted to know what forms of subsidy or subvention were paid in Cape Breton; he also wanted to know something about the Cape Breton national park, the roads to resources, including the Cabot trail, unemployment insurance for fishermen, fishing industry subsidies generally, construction or reconstruction of docks, harbours, breakwaters and dredges, assistance to industries in designated areas and, as well, he wanted to know something generally about coal and steel. I do not propose to go over the entire list. An answer was supplied to him, in which coal subventions were listed at $121 million. I have already said that over the last 38 years the assistance we received with respect to coal amounted to about $200 million. The answer to the question said, nevertheless, that total coal subventions were $121 million. A further $1,300,000 was paid in assistance toward the use of coal in the steel industry. That brings the total amount of assistance with respect to coal, according to the answer, to about $122 million.
Payments to the province with respect to development legislation, roads to resources and so on and so forth, added up to about $150 million. That was the figure that was spent in Cape Breton.
The impression that some might gain from such answers is totally false. Cape Breton does not depend on government assistance to any greater extent than any other parts of Canada depend on government assistance. Cape Bretoners are getting only what they are rightfully entitled to. But they only get it after making strong representations to the government with respect to those matters that were mentioned in the hon. members question.
Those in other areas of the country are able to get government help without making the strong representations that the representatives for Cape Breton have to make in the house. I could mention the art centre that is being built in Ottawa. While it was a hole in the ground, the building estimate rose from $19 million to between $38 million and $39 million. The people of Cape Breton ask for what any Canadian citizen is entitled to ask. On the other hand the art centre will not provide work. It is an amusement centre, and before it is finished I dare say that the government will have spent $50 million on it.
December 12, 1967

What about the $10 million that this government so generously allotted to establishing a film industry in this country. Look around you at the spending that has been going on. I appeal to you, gentlemen, to listen to me. I speak for a worthy cause. Make available to us the funds to renovate completely the Sydney steel operation, and let it stay in business.
My arguments get stronger as I go on, Mr. Speaker. I shall now refer to the building of the St. Lawrence seaway. That seaway was put into operation at the insistence of the government. It was put into operation over the protests of some in the maritimes, because the maritimes have port facilities.
Examine what the seaway has accomplished, Mr. Speaker. Something like $550 million was spent on seaway construction. Why was that money spent? After examining the remarks of members in this house, remarks which were made when the seaway was being promoted, I conclude that the seaway was not developed, primarily, for navigation purposes. I want it to be clearly understood that I do not wish to detract from any assistance that may be given to industries in other parts of the country. I conclude, Mr. Speaker, that the seaway was built, that the $550 million was spent, in order to subsidize that part of the country which is between Montreal and the lakehead.
A snow job was done with regard to many people at that time. The western farmer, because of the seaway, was to get 6 cents more per bushel for his wheat. I wonder what those members who are interested in western farm problems have to say about that? Can they say whether western farmers received that extra 6 cents per bushel as a result of the seaway having been built? The answer is obvious, I think. Every day we hear about the problems of the western farmer. Western farmers have difficulty in shipping their wheat, yet not once, so far as I am aware, has the question of ships been raised. Nor have I heard that in any way ships have been the cause of any delays. I never heard anything about the St. Lawrence seaway improving the situation. All I heard about was the same problem they had faced prior to this $550 million subsidy-lack of the box cars required to get grain as far as the seaway. So here we see a $550 million subsidy to assist this region.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
As I have said before, navigation was not the prime reason for building the seaway. I
The Budget-Mr. D. Maclnnis think the prime reason was to provide hydro power for Ontario, with possibly some power kickback to the province of Quebec, though Quebec apparently had plans for its own development. The idea that navigation was the reason for spending $550 million, the idea that this would assist western farmers, is down the drain. As a matter of fact the subsidy has returned nothing in this area; it has been a white elephant; the tolls realized on the seaway today do not even pay the interest on the money required to build it, and this situation will get worse because the Americans are developing ports along their east coast which will increasingly attract shipping away from the St. Lawrence.
When people talk about handouts to Cape Breton, let them look at the handout in connection with the seaway. As a matter of fact I do not regard it as a handout because I realize that although there were many objections raised to the project, in the considered opinion of the house, it was felt to be good for Canada-and being good for Canada it was also good for Nova Scotia. Today there is an opportunity to do something for Nova Scotia which will prove to be good in the long run for Canada.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I trust that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) is negotiating with Premier Smith he will adopt a generous attitude and provide the necessary funds to revitalize the Sydney steel industry.
It is very interesting to study the background of the building of the St. Lawrence seaway. I believe it was Senator Lodge of Massachusetts who said that the United States steel interests would all move out to the Atlantic coast. However, representations were made by the steel operators of Duluth, Indiana and Michigan to the effect that the United States government should participate in building the seaway in order that they might get cheaper ore from Canada and continue to produce steel in those areas. This is despite the fact that some United States senators were advocating moving the steel industry to the Atlantic coast.
It is also very interesting to bear in mind the argument put forward in favour of the building of the seaway by the late Right Hon. C. D. Howe, who had this to say in the United States: "We had to provide a St. Lawrence seaway, otherwise the steel industry
December 12, 1967

The Budget-Mr. D. Mciclnnis would move to the Atlantic coast." I emphasize this as a reason why the government is more or less obliged to come to the aid of the Sydney steel operation. So, what we have now is a $550 million subsidy provided for the area between Montreal and the lakehead, and one of the reasons put forward to justify it was to allow the operation of the steel industry in this country to remain in its traditional centres and keep it away from the Atlantic area. This is another good reason- and it was put forward by a former Liberal-why the government should be quick to come to the aid of the Sydney steel industry.
If Liberal members wish to do a little research they will find that one of the arguments put forward in favour of the subsidy was that the seaway would allow us to diversify the ship building industry, as carried on in Halifax, and move it to the lakehead.
One of the arguments put forward by the minister of transport at that time was that the seaway would permit the diversification of the shipbuilding industry. So the seaway was built for three or four different reasons. Again I emphasize that one of them was to prevent the steel operation going to the east coast. Another reason was to allow shipbuilding, which had been carried on almost exclusively on the east coast, to be carried on at the lakehead if and when shipbuilders decided to do so.
This is what has happened. The seaway has made it possible for the steel industry to continue to expand, to the detriment of the industry which had long been established at Sydney. At the same time, the seaway made it possible to diversify an industry which has its natural centre on the east coast, and move it to the lakehead.
I repeat, I am putting forward reasons why it is absolutely necessary that the federal government should respond generously at this time to the needs of Cape Breton. I am glad to see that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) is back in his place, because this is a subject which is of great concern to him and I am sure he will place all the arguments on behalf of the Sydney steel industry before his colleagues in the cabinet. It is my hope he will be able to convince the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters), who should be backing him up 100 per cent, and the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development (Mr. Sauve).
The subsidy which I have mentioned has acted to the detriment of the east coast. Let us turn now to other subsidies which have

been granted in a number of directions. I repeat that although coal has received assistance to the tune of $200 million over a period of 38 years, aid has been given to the uranium industry, which is an infant compared to the coal industry. Assistance was given to the uranium industry when it landed in trouble, to the tune of $150 million, over a much shorter period of time. I would call attention also to the assistance given to the gold mining industry under the emergency gold mining legislation. Since 1948 we have assisted the gold mining industry to the extent of some $231 million, not counting a possible further $15 million before the end of the present fiscal year. This represents assistance to the extent of $246 million.
Again, I have no objection to the assistance given to the industries I have mentioned, especially since it has been given because of the economic plight in which the people living in the mining areas would face if the work upon which they depend were lost to them. A similar situation faces the people in Sydney today.
May I call it ten o'clock?

PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS-REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF CANADA ELECTIONS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day I asked a question of the house leader, a question I have asked on more than one occasion. This had reference to the referral to the standing committee on privileges and elections of the Canada Elections Act. This is a procedure which normally follows a general election and, over the years, has proven to be a very useful one.
I may say I was not very pleased with the minister's answer, which at best was inadequate, and at worst was possibly arrogant and a bit discourteous. He said to me that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) had in fact answered the question which, by implication, suggested I had not been listening. Actually the Prime Minister's reply dealt with another matter, namely the referral of the report on the commission on election expenses. When I pointed out to the minister that he had not heard me correctly he casually, and a bit discourteously, said he had heard me correctly. If he heard me correctly he answered me incorrectly; he can have it either way.
This is a most important matter. The machinery whereby the electors elect their government is not a matter lacking in consequence in any well ordered political society. It is an important, a vital matter. The public must have the best opportunity to exercise their franchise, to vote properly, to have the best devices whereby they may register fully their points of view.
The elections act stands today without substantial review and without careful study by this committee. We have had three elections without a revision of it. Many problems have come up. Many submissions have come from citizens pointing out matters which they think are important.
We were led to believe in the speech from the throne that there would be a referral to committee of the report on election expenses. On May 8 we were told that when the study was completed the government would put forward proposals. These we have not yet seen. Away back in 1963, on December 20 of that year, the privileges and elections committee brought in a report to this house which contained a paragraph saying the committee recommended that it be empowered to study the Canada Elections Act at the earliest possible date next session, with a view to affording the committee an opportunity for exhaustive and constructive examination and study of that act. That was in 1963;

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion but that call for an early opportunity has gone unheeded.
We are in a uniquely difficult situation as a result of the Representation Act, whereby there are new returning officers and new districts. Surely we do not want to add to their difficulty by having the elections act amended at the last moment.
It is always imprudent to have the election machinery rusty, but in a situation where you have a minority government, where there could be an appeal to the people at any moment, it is a shocking situation of neglect. We do not know what might happen, but if you look over the history of this government in recent years and see how accident prone it has been, we can see the only accident it has not suffered is a major defeat in this house; and by this I mean something more substantial than on the postal resolution. If such a defeat came we would not have an up to date Canada Elections Act.
Many problems arose in November, 1965. Thousands of our students found that the regulations did not provide them with a chance to vote. Civil servants abroad have constantly requested some machinery whereby they may register their franchise. This has been brought before the committee time and time again. I would hope there would be an opportunity for the committee to recommend, and for the house to adopt, a broader provision, covering not just civil servants and external affairs officers but providing for an absentee vote that would give an opportunity for Canadians abroad, in a general category, to exercise their franchise.
For years we have talked about a permanent list whereby long election campaigns could be shortened. This is the kind of thing to which we should be applying ourselves. I think it is disgraceful; it is neglectful, it is imprudent; it is unwise. If I were the Secretary of State I would say that the fact that nothing has been done about this is an indication of rotten management. We find that the committee has not been constituted. No chairman has been designated. Some of us are becoming weary of calling the government to task in this regard. We would hope that in this area at least they would discard the languid approach and regard the election machinery as something pretty important to a responsible government. I would hope that the step of having referred to the committee for study more than the matter of the age of voting might be taken forthwith.
December 12, 1967

As my hon. friend knows, we have sent at least one resolution affecting the voting age to this committee. The government expects to send the report on election expenses to this committee before the end of this session, and I hope at an early date. With regard to the elections act, I agree with the hon. member that it is desirable that this act be considered by the committee at the earliest possible date. It may not be possible to have a committee study of the elections act at this session, but certainly it will be considered very early in the next session.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 29 on the orders of the day I asked the Prime Minister whether the government would keep the centennial flame burning after the end of the year as a symbol of Canadian unity. When Mr. Speaker ruled that he did not consider the question to be sufficiently urgent to be answered during the question period I immediately gave notice that I wished to raise it on an adjournment debate. This is the first convenient time this could be done.
I asked my question on November 29 by way of expressing my view that the flame should not be snuffed out permanently on December 31. I felt, and subsequent events proved that I was correct, that this view was shared by most of the members of this house and by millions of other Canadians as well.
I think I should indicate at this time, for the record at least, that I had the privilege of raising this question in the house on the orders of the day perhaps a week before a similar question was put by a member of one of the opposition parties. His question was also not accepted by Mr. Speaker at that time. I do not think I would be giving away any secrets if I said that, joined particularly by other members on this side of the house, I continued my efforts through direct contacts with the Prime Minister and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith) to have the government's original decision not to continue the flame reversed.
[Mr. MacquarrieJ
Therefore, I was pleased to note the information in the answer given to the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) yesterday by the Prime Minister, that the flame would be continued. After all, there are as yet all too few monuments which stand as tangible symbols of Canada as a nation and which are accepted as such by the public at large. The flame has proven to be one of these. Although it was intended only as a symbol of centennial year, the flame immediately became looked upon by the public at large as something more-as a symbol of Canada as a nation.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
If any proof of this is required, it has been provided by the way it has drawn almost every visitor to the hill, from the first day it was ignited by the Prime Minister almost a year ago. Further proof has been provided by the public protest when it appeared the flame would be extinguished as of December 31 of this year. To have extinguished this flame at that time could very likely have been interpreted, though wrongly interpreted, by some elements of the press and public as symbolizing in a negative way, again quite wrongly, the fate of our country. However, if this flame continues to burn it can and will be a tangible gesture demonstrating our faith as representatives of the people of this country in the continuing existence of a united Canada from sea to sea.
The Prime Minister has now said that the flame will continue, but I think there are two further points to be made at this time. A press report today suggests that the flame may be moved away from parliament hill to another point in Ottawa. I think this would be the wrong thing to do. The symbolic effect would not be the same if the flame continued to burn at some location other than parliament hill; at another site. Is there a better place than parliament hill for such a flame? After all, it is a place for the coming together of the people of this country as Canadians; it is the focal point of their aspirations and hopes, as Canadians. The parliament buildings provide a fitting background for the flame which could not be found at any other place in Ottawa.
The second point I wish to make is that I have heard that private interests have indicated their interest in providing the cost of continuing the flame. While I understand the good intentions behind such an offer, in my opinion it would be more appropriate if this flame were maintained, not by special

interests, but by the Canadian people. Some may raise a question about the cost of having the flame continued, but there would be in any event the sizeable cost of dismantling the mechanism for the flame and repaving the roadway. I am confident that the cost would be very small in comparison to other expenditures that are being made, and if we wanted to I am sure we could come up with ways of tightening up on some of these other expenditures to make up the amounts required. But I am sure the cost at most would be small compared with the symbolic benefits.
When the mayor of Montreal spoke at the closing of Expo he said in effect: Expo is gone, but long live man and his world. The new decision of the government about the flame will enable the Prime Minister to say on December 31: The flame of the centennial will be gone, but this flame at the same time will live on as a memento of centennial year; but, more important, it will be a symbol of Canadian unity and our faith in the Canada of tomorrow.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to hear the hon. member speak as he has spoken. I am sure that hon. members will feel that the centennial celebrations have somehow created a new pride and faith in the hearts of Canadians. It seems to me that this centennial flame has become a symbol of this pride and faith in Canadianism.
A decision has been made to continue the flame in perpetuity. The question will ultimately have to be decided as to what if anything should be done to improve the layout of the plaza surrounding it. It has been placed on a walk adjacent to a road that was not designed to accommodate the traffic pattern on the hill today. It may be found that

Parts of this will have to be replaced and may involve redesign and the use of different materials. At no time has there been any question that the cost of maintenance of the flame was of such magnitude that it should be discontinued for this reason. That has never been put forward or suggested by anyone.
The question which must be decided is related to the best way to preserve this symbol, which has become well known throughout our centennial celebrations, and how to preserve it during the new century which we are entering. We may at some later time take a decision as to its possible relocation. If you examine its location carefully you will see that at some future time this may have to be reconsidered.
Let me give an illustration of what I have in mind. It has been suggested that when the new museum is designed for location in the central part of the city the landscaping could be such that this centennial flame could be placed at its entrance to great advantage.
All I am trying to indicate is that at the start of a new century in Canada's history it is not wise, perhaps, to make a final decision as to the precise site of a flame of the importance of this one. In any event, the decision is that it will be left exactly where it is for the time being, and these other questions will have to be decided later. I believe that news should be pleasing to all hon. members. As a matter of fact, I am surprised by what has gone out in the news in the last days and weeks. It has got a little out of hand. However, Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to go into this aspect of the matter tonight.
